caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 744 of 1999
lawyer:
For the Petitioner: Mr. Abdur Razzaq, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. 
Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record. 
Respondent No. 1: Mr. Fida Kamal, Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record. 
Respondent Nos. 2-3: Not represented.
parties:
Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited ----- Petitioner
Versus 
Haji Bashiruddin and Others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Latifur Rahman, J. This petition for leave to appeal by Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited plaintiff petitioner is against the judgment and order passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 6.5.99 in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 75 of 1995 reversing the order dated 13.3.95 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 1992 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

2. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 23 of 1991 on 21.1.91 against the respondents in the Court of Subordinate Judge and 3rd Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka for recovery of a sum of Tk. 89,32,300/-. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 20.6.91. Thereafter on 23.3.92 defendant No. 3 filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree alleging that summons were sup-pressed and he came to know of the ex parte decree in the later part of February, 1992 and within 30 days from the date of knowledge he filed the miscellaneous case. 

3. The plaintiff petitioner filed a written objection stating that summons were duly served upon defendant No. 3 and he deliberately did not appear in the case. The miscellaneous case was filed long after 276 days from the order of ex parte decree. Hence the miscellaneous case should not be allowed. 

4. As already noticed, the trial court dismissed the miscellaneous case and the High Court Division allowed the miscellaneous case and restored the suit to its file and number after awarding as cost of Tk. 25,000/- against the respondent. 

5. Mr. Abdur Razzaq, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff bank petitioner submits that in this case summons were duly served and as such the High Court Division wrongly restored the suit after allowing miscellaneous case. 
He next submits that there being a delay of 276 days from the date of ex parte decree the miscellaneous case ought not to have been allowed by the Division Bench of the High Court Division. 

6. In the judgment of the trial court there is no consideration at all whether the summons was served upon the defendant or not. It is the definite case of the defendant that summons of the original suit was never served upon him and by suppression of the summons ex parte decree was obtained. The learned Judges of the High Court Division found that the plaintiff did not examine any witness including the process server to prove the service of summons upon the defendant. The learned Judges of the High Court Division believed the story of defendant that he came to know of the ex parte decree in the later part of February, 1992 and filed the miscellaneous case within 30 days of his knowledge. In that view of the matter, the miscellaneous case was allowed by the Division Bench after awarding a cost of Tk. 25,000/-against the defendant. The learned Judges of the High Court Division having exercised discretion, we do not think that this is a proper case for our interference. 

7. The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Mahbubey Alam with Mr. Md. Ekramul Islam -- For the petitioners
Mr. Mohammad Mostafa -- For the opposite party No 1
parties:
Md. Azizul Islam and another ----- Petitioners
Versus
Sheikh Shamsur Rahman and others ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Mohammad Abdur Rashid, J : This Rule was obtained by defendant No 10 and 11 upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against Order No 36 dated 05.09.2000 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No 1 at Jessore in Title Suit No 24 of 1997, which refused the prayer for rejection of the plaint. 

2. Opposite party No 1 as plaintiff instituted the suit against the petitioners and opposite parties No 2 to 12 for specific performance of an agreement --1.2tca 07.03.96. By an agreement further reief for declaration that the Compromise decree dated 25.11.97 passed in Title Suit No 6 of 1995 is collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff, and also for setting aside the decree on finding that there was no agreement between the defendants No 1 to 9 and defendants No 10 to 11. Plaint case, in short, is that one Ismat Ara Khadija was owner in possession of the suit land. She died leaving a husband. defendant No 1, three sons defendants No. 2 to 4 and five daughters defendants No. 5 to 9. Defendant No 2 to 9 appointed their father defendant No 1 as their attorney by a power of attorney dated 21.01.74. On 07.03.96 defendant No 1 on his behalf and on behalf of defendant No 2 to 9 agreed to sell the suit land at a consideration of Taka 8,00,000/- to the plain-tiff and on receipt of Taka 2,00,000/- by way of Bank Draft executed an agreement and delivered possession. It was also stipulated that after the disposal of Title Suit No 6 of 1995, the defendants would exe-cute and register necessary deed of sale on receipt of the balance of the consideration. 

3. On 04.11.98 the petitioners made an application under Order 7 Rule 11(a)(b) of the Code for rejection of the plaint. In the application it is stated that defendants No 1 to 9 on 02.06.94 entered into an agreement with the petitioners for sale of the suit land at a consideration of Taka 3.20,000/-, pursuant to the agreement, defendants No. 1 to 9 having failed to exe-cute and register the deed of sale, the petitioners were constrained on 14.02.95 to institute Title Suit No 6 of 1995 for specific performance of contract. On 25.11.97 the suit was decreed on compromise and in execution of the decree: 21 Title Execution No 1 of 1097 on 15.03.98 they got a kabala duly executed and registered. It is further stated that the plaintiff having full knowledge and notice of the said agreement` and the title suit entered into the aforesaid agreement on 07.03.96 in respect of the selfsame land with the self-same vendors during the pendency of the suit and thereby, they are bound by the result i.e. the decree of the suit. 

4. As stated above, the application was heard and rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge being of the view whether or not the plaintiff and defendants No. 1 to 9 entered into any agreement and whether or not the agreement. it any, could be enforced: and secondly, whether or not the compromise decree dated 30.11.97 is collusive, fraudulent or not binding upon the plaintiff can only be decided at the trial on evidence. 

5. Mr. Mahbubey Alam learned Senior Advocate has reads out the agreement dated 07.03.96 and submits that the plaintiff having entered into the agreement with full knowledge of the agreement dated 02.06.94 and Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 instituted for enforcement of the earlier agreement and the suit having been decreed and kabala duly executed and registered on the basis of the decree, the plaintiff is neither protected under the provision of section 27(b) nor he can maintain the suit for specific performance of the subsequent agreement in respect of the selfsame suit land against the self-same vendors. He accordingly submits that the plaintiff has got no cause of action for the first relief as prayed for in the suit. In support he cites the decision in the case of Momtazul Karim Vs. Abul Hossain, (1970) 22 DLR 146. Secondly he submits that in view of the provisions of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act by entering into an agreement for purchase the plaintiff acquired no interest in the suit land and as such, he has got neither any legal character nor any right to maintain a suit for declaration against the decree dated 25.11.97. In support, he relied upon the decision in the case of Burmah Eastern Vs. B. E. Employees Union (1966) 18 DLR 709 and that of Abdul Jalil Vs. Islami Bank Limited. (2001) 53 DLR (AD) 12. Concluding, he submits that the learned Subordinate Judge wholly misconceived the scope of the application and erred in law in resulting to reject the plaint. 

6. Mr. Mohammad Mostafa, learned Advocate for the Opposite Party No. 1 submits that plaintiff by entering into the agreement dated 07.03.96 and into the possession of the land on the basis of an agreement has acquired some possessory right which he is always entitled to defend. He further submits that in view of the pro-vision of Section 53(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, the plaintiff is always entitled to defend his possession. Accordingly, the plaint of the suit could not be thrown away in limini before the trial. He relied upon the decision in the case of Dr. Mohammad Hossain Vs. A. Malik Khan, (1980) 32 DLR(AD) 24. 

7. We have perused the revision application, the plaint, the application for rejection of the plaint, the agreement dated 07.03.96 and the affidavits filed on behalf of the parties. Facts as stated above are not disputed. In the suit, the plaintiff now seeks for two distinct reliefs one for enforcement of the agreement dated 07.03.96 and the other one is a declamatory one for declaring the decree dated 25.11.97 passed in Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 illegal, collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff, and also for setting aside the decree on a decision that there was no agreement between defendants No. 1 to 9 and defendants No 10 to 11 which was subsequently added by an amending application dated 07.04.99. Cause of action for the suit as given in the plaint is the date of the agreement dated 07.03.96 and date of the decree obtained by the petitioners dated 25.11.97 and his knowledge as on 26.12.97 about the decree. 

8. The agreement dated 07.03.96 clearly reads to the effect that on 07.03.96 defendant No. 9 on his behalf and on behalf of defendants No. 1 to 8 received a Bank Draft of Taka 2,00,000/- and delivered possession of the suit land to the plaint. It is clearly stipulated that after the disposal of Title Suit No. 6 of 1995. and receipt of rest of the consideration of Taka 6,00.000/- the defendant No. 1 to 9 would execute and register necessary deed of also conveying title. It is also stated that said defendants never entered into any agreement on which the Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 is pending. It is also stated in the agreement that having full knowledge of the said suit, both parties accordingly bound themselves into the agreement. On behalf of defendant No. 1 to 9 defendant No. 9 and the plaintiff executed the agreement in presence of the witnesses. In view of such stipulations the plaintiff binds himself and also the fact of his agreement dated 07.03.96 with the result of Title Suit No. 6 of 1995. 

9. After the decree in the and necessary died of also executed and registered in execution of the decree title of defendant No. 1 to 9 in the suit land already conveyed to those petitioners. Said defendants are now possession of no title in respect of the suit land. Subsequently suit for a deed of sale from the same vendors is fore doomed. Had this plaintiff been a party in the earlier suit as a: subsequent transferee he would have been obliged to join defendants No. 1 to 9 to execute and register the deed of sale conveying title of the suit land on he basis of the decree passed on 25.11.97 under the provisions of Section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. Under the provisions of Section 27(b) the interest of the plaintiff not at all protected since he entered into subsequent agreement in respect of the self-same land with the selfsame vendors with full knowledge and notice of the agreement and also the suit brought for enforcement of the said agreement, Section 53(a) of the Transfer of Property does not entitle such a plaintiff to Maintain a suit for specific performance of his subsequent agreement. Nor he can defend his possession, if any. he got on the basis of his agreement in view of the decision in the case of Momtazul Karim Vs. Abul Hossain (1970) 22 DLR 146. 

10. Secondly; by entering into such agreement on 07.03.96 with the defendants No. 1 to 9 the plaintiff acquired no right nor any lawful interest in the suit land. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act has clearly provided that con-tract for sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties. It does not of itself clear any interest in or change on such property. When the plaintiff did not acquire any right in the suit land nor did he acquire any legal character under any law by such transaction, he is not a person within the meaning of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act to be entitled to seek for a declaration against the decree dated 25.11.1997. 

11. Mr. Mostafa very much relied upon the decision in the case of Mohammad Hossai7 Vs. A. Malik (1980) 32 DLR (AD) 24. There the question arose on the quantum of share among three joint decree holders who obtained the decree jointly in enforcement of a contract, and all of them admittedly ,/ere in possession of the land decreed. There the Appellate Division was of the view that there may be various species of possessory or legal rights created on the property which can be enforced. Once there is a legal right, the remedy will be available according to right. Observation was solely based on the decree obtained by the parties. Here the plaintiff stands on a mere agreement which was also entered into with full knowledge of the earlier agreement and the suit brought for enforcement of the agreement. So, this decision will be of no help to the plaintiff.

12. In such facts and circumstances of the case and of the law, the plaintiff has got no cause of action for the instant suit. Long ago in the case of Burmah Eastern. a Division Bench ruled that in the absence of any legal interest, character or right one is not entitled to maintain a suit under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. If the suit turns out to be a still born that should be properly buried at its earliest inception. Lastly, our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Jalil Vs. Islam' Bank Limited took the view that when the ultimate result of a suit as is clear as daylight that such a suit should be buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in fruitless litigation. We are also convinced, the plaintiff has got no case. His fate is sealed by his own conduct and stand as he has taken in the plaint. This Division cannot allow such misconceived, frivolous and vexatious suit to continue any more. 

13. In the above view of the case, we find learned Subordinate Judge totally misconceived the scope of the application made under Order 7 Rule 11. When the fate of the suit is deemed there is no scope for inquiry whether or not the con-tract was genuine or the contract could be enforced or the plaintiff would be entitled to a decree for a declaration as sought for. So, there is no escape from the conclusion that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to exercise the jurisdiction vested in him under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code in rejecting the plaint of a misconceived and vexatious suit at its earliest. The impugned order has therefore, resulted in serious failure of justice.

14. In the result, this Rule is made absolute without however, any order as to costs. The impugned order is set aside. The plaint of Title Suit No. 24 of 1997 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Jessore is hereby rejected. 

15. The order of stay granted earlier is hereby re-called and vacated. 

Communicate. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.115 of 1996
lawyer:
For the Petitioner: Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, Advocate on Record, Supreme Court. 
Respondents: Not represented.
parties:
M. A. Salek (Salauddin) ------ Plaintiff-Petitioner.
Versus
Sree Sree Kripaymaya Kali Mata & others ------ Defendant-Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdur Rouf J.: The plaintiff-petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 92 of 1987 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of possession of the suit properties stating, inter alia, that the same originally belonged to the Roads and Highways Division of the Government of Bangladesh that by executing registered kabuliat dated 16.8.84 he took lease of the same from them, that about 52 persons, members of Dokan Babosthapona Samity Joydevpur, have been possessing the same and that on 25.11.86 the defendants forcibly dispossessed them there from.

	2. The suit on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 53 of 1989 of the Court of the Additional Assistant Judge Gazipur in the ex-parte disposal of the suit the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the same on 7.2.90. But in Civil Revision 962 of 1990, preferred by the petitioner, a Single Bench of the High Court. Division on 7.2.91 decreed the suit making the Rule absolute. The Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 1992 preferred by the Government of Bangladesh against the aforesaid judgment of the High Court Division was dismissed on 5.8.93. The petitioner however instituted Execution Case No. 1 of 1992 which was stayed by the executing court on the pendency of the leave petition. On 2-9-93 the petitioner by filing application prayed for proceeding with the said execution case. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2. claiming themselves as the representative of the Deity, Sree Kripaymaya Kali Mata, as 3rd party filed on 4-9-93 an application under Order XXI Rules 26 and 29 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying to stay further proceeding of the said execution case pending disposal of Title Suit No. 225 of 1986 of the court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur stating. Inter-alia, that the aforesaid suit was filed by the Deity in 1980 for declaration of her title to the suit land as Title Suit No. 1065 of 1980 of the Court of Subordinate Judge first Court. Dhaka and that the present petitioner at his own instance was added as defendant in that suit, and that on 22.11.1980 the said subordinate Judge passed an order in respect of the suit land for maintaining status quo pending disposal of the suit and the said suit is shit pending for disposal and that the present petitioner in his plaint although had mentioned the institution of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 1065 of 1980 but intentionally did not make the said Deity or her aforesaid representatives as party in his suit. 

	3. The executing court after hearing both the parties by an order dated 18.9.9'? stayed further proceeding of the execution case pending disposal of Title Suit No. 225 of 1986. The petitioner then preferred Civil Revision No. 2096 of 1993 against that order. A Single Bench of the High Court Division on 14-8-95 maintained the order of the executing court by discharging the Rule on contest. 

	4. The petitioner is now seeking leave to appeal from the said judgment of the High Court Division.

	5. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the petitioner submitted that the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in holding that the executing court upon proper exercise of his authority under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure rightly stayed the further proceeding of the execution case in question pending disposal of T.S. No. 225 of 1986. 

	6. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as representatives of the aforesaid Deity on 15.11.80 instituted Title Suit No. 1065 of 1980 (subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 225 of 1986) against the Government and others for declaration of her title to the suit land claiming exclusive possession therein on the basis of a registered deed of endowment dated 3.11.1913 said to have been made by the then Zaminder of Bhawal, namely kripa-mayee Devi for religious purpose of the Hindu Community of the locality. The petitioner on 27-8-82 got himself added as defendant No. 6 therein. The suit is still pending. This Division dismissed C.P. No. 216 of 1992 on 15.8.93, preferred by the Government against the decree passed by the High Court Division in revision (C.R. 962/90) on the ground that the Government's possession if any would not be affected by that decree in question. The executing court in the impugned order has noted that in pending Civil Revision Nos. 1709/91, 1593/92, arising out of the aforesaid Title Suit No.225 of 1986, the High Court Division's orders of maintaining status quo In respect of the suit land are still in force, that the present Petitioner is a party in those cases and that the petitioner in his suit did not implead the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 225 of 1986 as party. 

	7. Thus the learned Judge of the High Court Division in the facts and circum-stances of the case has rightly refused to interfere with the discretion exercised by the executing court under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the interest of justice staying further proceeding of the execution case pending disposal of Title Suit No. 225 of 1986. We do not find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division which war-rants any interference. The petition is also barred by one day for which no application for condonation has been filed. 

	8. The petition is, therefore, dismissed. 
	End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 741 with 960 of 2000
lawyer:
For the petitioners (In both the petitions): Mr. Fazlul Karim, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record. 

For Respondent Nos. 1-15 (in CP No. 741/2000) Respondent No. 1-14 (In CP No. 960/2000): Mr. Gabinda Chandra Tagor, Advocate (appeared with the leave of the Court), instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record. 

Respondent Nos. 16-136 (In CP No. 741/2000): Not Represented. Respondent Nos. 15-36 (In CP No. 960/2000): Not Represented.
parties:
Makhan Baral and another ------ Petitioners (In CP No. 741/2000)
Parfullah Mazi & another ------ Petitioners (In CP No. 960/2000)
-Versus-
Shaylendra Nath Mondal and others ------ Respondents (In CP No. 741/2000)
Bantu Rana and others ------ Respondents (In CP No. 960/2000)
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Ruhul Amin, J: These two leave petitions have been filed by two sets of judgment-debtors. In leave petition No. 741 of 2000 judgment-debtors-petitioners are opposing the Execution Case No. 1 of 1996, which has been filed for execution of the decree that was passed on 18 August 1960 (decree was signed on 24 August 1960), in Title Suit No. 143 of 1952 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) Bagerhat which was for declaration of title and kash possession in respect of 55 bighas of land, contending, inter alia, that the execution case is barred by limitation and that also barred under Section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance No. 10 of 1984. that the suit land is unspecified, that in schedule No. 1 decree-holders are claiming 30 bighas of land instead of 20 bighas of land and that in schedule No. 2 they are claiming 55 bighas of land in place of 35 bighas of land and thereupon in total they are claiming 75 bighas of land in place of 55 bighas of land for which decree was passed in the aforementioned title suit that 30/35 persons are residing on the land on the strength of settlement taken in March 1987 that execution case is liable to be rejected since suit was filed before the Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) but the execution case has been filed before the Subordinate Judge. 

	2. Judgment-debtors-petitioners in Leave Petition No. 960 of 2000 are opposing the Execution Case No. 2 of 1996 which has been filed for execution of the decree dated 18th August. 1960 (decree signed on 25th August 1960) in Title Suit No. 206 of 1951 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (Now Assistant Judge) which was for declaration of title and khas possession in respect of 29 bighas, or in other words 7 acres of land, contending inter alia, that decree holders 1.5.8.9.10.11.12 and 14 are not residing in Bangladesh and that they have not authorized the decree-holder respondents to represent them in the execution case, that the land is unspecified. that decree-holders have filed Execution Case as regard land which is excess of the decretal land, that 10/15 persons arc residing in the land taking settlement front Government in 1987, that under Section 6 of the Land Reforms Ordinance No. 10 of 1984 settlement holders cannot evicted and that execution is barred by limitation. 

	3. The objections so raised by the judgment-debtors in Execution Case No. 1 of 1996 and No. 2 of 1996 were rejected by the learned Assistant Judge, in-charge, Chittalmari, Bagerhat by the Order No. 35 dated 14.9.1999 and Order No. 36 dated 14.9.1999 respectively. 

	4. Judgment-debtors as against the aforesaid respective order moved the High Court Division in civil revisional juris-diction and thereupon obtained Rules, being Civil Revision No. 4295 of 1999 against the Order No. 35 dated 14.9.99 and Civil Revision No. 4296 of 1999 against Order No. 36 dated 14.9.1999. 

	5. The Civil Rules were heard together and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rules by the judgment and order dated 5 June 2000. 

	6. Mr. Fazlul Karim, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners in Leave Petition No. 741 of 2000 submits that the learned Single Judge was in error in not noticing the vital fact that although decree-holders (respondent Nos. 1-15 herein) obtained decree in respect of 20 bighas of land in the 1st schedule and 35 bighas of land in the 2nd Schedule but they have put the decree into execution for 30 bighas of land in 1st schedule and thereupon have put the decree into execution for total quantity of 65 bighas of land although they have obtained decree of 55 bighas of land. 

	7. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the petitioners in Leave Petition No. 960 of 2000 has submitted that execution case cannot be proceeded with as good number of decree-holders are not residing in Bangladesh. 

	8. As against the aforesaid submissions the learned Counsel entering into caveat for the decree-holder-respondents has submitted that the contention making which, i.e. decree-holders have filed the execution case for 30 bighas of land in 1st Schedule instead of 20 bighas of land for which decree has been obtained and that in the execution case in total claiming 65 bighas of land instead of 55 bighas of land judgment-debtors opposing the execution are totally incorrect in that in the execution application there were some typographical mistake as to quantity of land in the 1st schedule and that as to total quantity of land and that same has been corrected upon filing an application tor amendment. The learned Advocate to substantiate the said submission, has referred to the execution application, as in the additional paper book, that stands after the amendment. 

	9. The learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners in Leave Petition No. 741 of 2000 having noticed the said fact felt difficulty to press the contention as to filing of execution for excess quantity of land contrary to the decree obtained in the suit as mentioned above and thereupon did not proceed further on that count. The other contention of the learned Counsel is that in case the execution is allowed 30-35 persons would be rendered shelter less and that in view of the provisions of Land Reform Ordinance No. 10 of 1984 such eviction is barred. He has further sub-mitted that decree-holders having not put the decree for kash possession upon demolition of the structures the execution ease cannot be proceeded. The submissions of the learned Counsel merit no consideration since persons who are claiming to be on the land upon erecting structures came therein much much long after the decree obtained and that as seen from the materials on the record the said persons came some time in 1987. The submissions of the learned Counsel appearing in Leave Petition No. 960 of 2000 as to that some of the decree-holders are outside the country is also of no substance in that the decree that has been obtained in the title suit admittedly a joint one obtained by several persons and that no special condition has been attached to the decree so obtained disentitling any one of the decree-holders to apply for the execution of the decree in its entirety for the benefits of all the decree-holders or that for the benefit of the survivors and the legal representatives of the decree-holders. 

	10. In view of the discussions made hereinabove there is no substance in the contention upon which Leave Petitioners are seeking leave to appeal. 

	11. The learned Advocate entering into caveat for the decree-holders has submitted that the judgment-debtors have filed Leave Petition No. 741 of 2000 against the judgment and order dated 5 June, 2000 in Civil Revision No. 4295 of 2000 as well as the said civil revision against the Order No. 35 dated 14 September, 1999 passed in Execution Case No. 1 of 1996 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Chittalmari, Bagerhat upon using the fabricated certified copy of the Execution application upon which Execution Case No. 1 of 1996 was registered, showing that the decree-holders have filed Execution Case for 30 bighas of land in the 1st schedule and for total quantity of 65 bighas of land as the decretal land instead of 55 bighas of land. It is the undisputed position that petitioners in the Leave Petition No. 741 of 2000 as well as in the Civil Revision No. 4295 of 2000 moved the Appellate Division and the High Court Division of the Supreme Court primarily contending that decree-holders put the decree into execution showing excess land as the decretal land and that to substantiate said contention used certified copy of execution application where upon Execution Case No. 1 of 1996 was registered which ultimately was, found contrary to actual state of matter. The judgment-debtors being unsuccessful in the High Court Division as to their contention of filing the execution case for 30 bighas of land in the st schedule on the basis of the certified copy of the execution application used by the judgment-debtors in the High Court Division. they again have filed leave petition using the said fabricated certified copy of the execution application showing 30 .bighas of land in 1st schedule of the Execution application upon the assertion that said certified copy of the application for execution is a genuine one in spite of knowing the same not being genuine, rather fabricated and thereupon the learned Advocate entering into caveat has submitted that thereby the said judgment-debtors-petitioners in the aforementioned Civil Revision No. 4295 of 1999 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 741 of 2000 having had committed offence as mentioned in Section 195(1)(c) of Cr.P.C. the Registrar of this Court or any other Officer as authorized by the Registrar as per provision of Section 476A of .the Code of Criminal Procedure be directed to make a complaint against the judgment-debtors petitioners of Civil Leave Petition No. 741 of 2000 to the Magistrate, Bagerhat for committing offence under Section 195(1)(c) of the Penal Code for using fabricated documents genuine. Respondent Nos. 1-15 (decree-holders) in that respect have filed an application before this Division. In view of the materials on record and that as there is substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate entering into caveat for the decree-holder respondent Nos. 1-15 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 741 of 2000 we are of the view that the application filed under Section 476A Cr.P.C. on behalf of the decree-holder-respondent Nos. 1-15 for making com-plaint to the Magistrate for committing offence said to be under one of the sections of the Penal Code as mentioned in Section 195(1)(c) of the Cr.P.0 merits consideration. Accordingly the Registrar of this Court is directed to send the application filed under Section 476A Cr.P.0 filed by the decree-holder-respondent Nos. 1-15 before this Division to the Court of the learned Assistant Judge Chittalmari, Bagerhat authorizing him to take steps in accordance with law for initiation of the proceeding under any one of the section of the Penal Code as mentioned in 195(1)(c) of the Cr.P.C. 

	12. As we do not find any merit in the light of our discussions made hereinbefore the leave petitions are dismissed. 

	13. The application filed under Section 476A Cr.P.C. by the decree-holder respondent Nos. 1-15 in the light of aforesaid direction be sent to the learned Assistant Judge, Chittalmari, Bagerhat to take necessary steps.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 516 of 1996
lawyer:
For petitioner: Mr. Md, Fazlul Karim, Senior Advocate instructed by Mr. Md. Nawab Ali. Advocate-on-Record. 
For respondentNos.1-2, 4-8 and 10-12 : Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on Record.

Respondent Nos. 3, 9,13-23: Not represented.
parties:
Sharif Abdul Mannan Petitioner
Versus
Mst. Motahara Banu and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.: This petition for leave to appeal by the defendant petitioner is from the judgment and order dated 25-6-96 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2091 of 1993 discharging the Rule. 

	2. The plaintiff respondents filed Title Suit No.88 of 1993 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for partition. They filed an application for amendment of the plaint which was allowed by the trial Court by order No. 144 dated 5-7-93. By the said amendment the plaintiffs prayed for a new relief in the plaint to the effect that they be allowed a decree to purchase the share of defendant, No 8, Sharif Abdul Mannan and consequential relief be passed in pursuance thereof. The Rule issued in the petitioner's civil revision case was discharged. 

	3. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for defendant No. 8-petitioner, reiterates the submission which he made unsuccessfully before the High Court, Division, namely, that the relief sought for cannot be considered by the trial Court as a relief in the suit itself and that the plain-tiffs ought to have filed a miscellaneous case under Section 4 of the partition Act in case the suit is decreed for partition in a preliminary form. The amended prayer was made prematurely. Item No. 36 under Rule 77 in Civil Rules and Orders provides for registration of cases under Sections 2,3 and 4 of the partition Act as miscellaneous judicial cases. There is no scope for praying for any relief in the suit itself in terms of Section 4 of the partition Act. 

	4. The High Court Division held that the plaintiffs can pray for such relief at the initial stage by including the relief in the plaint itself or at any stage subsequent thereto. The only entitlement of defendant No.8 is to file an additional written statement and also to get a reasonable cost from the plaintiffs for filing an additional written statement. 

	5. We do not think that the High Court Division committed any error of law in holding the said view. 

	6. In that view of the matter the petition is dismissed. 

	End.

Latifur Rahman, J: This petition by defendant-petitioners is directed against the judgment and order dated 25.3.98 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2004 of 1995 setting aside the order dated 15.3.95 passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 1992 refusing those dated 2.9.98 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Case No. 78 of 1991 arising out of an application under Order-9 Rule-13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 49 of 1990 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Satkhira. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 15.10.91. After the disposal of the suit the defendant-petitioners filed an application under Order-9 Rule-13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree alleging that no notice and summons were served upon them in the original suit and that the plaintiffs obtained the ex parte decree by suppressing the summons/notices in collusion with the process server of the Court. The defendant on 29.10.91 for the first time came to know about the ex parte decree from one Dinabandhu Gosh and thereafter filed the miscellaneous case for setting aside the ex parte decree. 
The plaintiff-respondents asserted in their written objection that summons/ notices of the suit were duly served upon the defendants. The defendants were aware of the suit and there was no suppression of summons and notices nor any forgery was practiced in the matter of service of summons. 

3. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not construing the provisions of Rules 17 and 19 of Order-5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and wrongly held that there was due service of summons/ notices in the present case and refused to set aside the ex parte decree. 

4. In this case, P.W.2 the process server appeared and testified that summons were duly served. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that apart from the declaration on the return of process server that summons were duly served, notices with acknowledgement dues were posted in the correct addresses of the defendants. The return of acknowledgement dues with postal endorsement clearly showed that notices were refused by the defendants. It is on record that along with service of summons, simultaneously notices with postal acknowledgement dues were sent in the correct addresses of the defendants. Apart from this, the defendants stated that they came to know about the ex parte decree from one Dinabandhu in presence of Rabindra Nath Biswas but curiously enough the said Dinabandhu was not examined by the defendants. The question of taking recourse to Rules 17 and 19 of Order 5 does not arise in the present case. The learned Single Judge having taken a correct view of law the same calls for no interference. 
5. The petition is dismissed. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. S. K. Sinha, J: This revisional application is directed against the order dated 24.1.2002 of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 2001 setting aside the ex parte decree dated 5.7.2001 passed in title suit No. 201 of 1999. 

2. Petitioner instituted the suit for declaration of title in respect of the suit property. The suit ultimately came up for pre-emptory hearing, the petitioner was examined on commission and thereafter on 5.7.2001 the suit was decreed ex parte. The opposite parties filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. on 15.7.2001 for setting aside the ex parte decree. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 2001. The learned Assistant Judge upon hearing the parties, by the impugned order \dated 24.1.2002 allowed the Miscellaneous case and restored the suit to its file and number. 

3. Mr. Nikhilesh Dutta, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in restoring the suit on setting aside the ex parte decree in the absence of any evidence on record that the defendants were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing.

 4. I have perused the application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C., the written objection filed by the petitioner against the said application and the impugned order. The learned Assistant Judge restored the suit on the reasonings that since the defendant opposite parties had been contesting the suit ends of justice demands that the defendants should be afforded an opportunity to contest the suit subject to payment of Tk. 600/- as costs within 30 days from the date of the order. 

5. True, the learned Assistant Judge allowed the application and set aside the ex parte decree in a summary manner without examining any witness. It is also fact that the suit was decreed ex parte on 5.7.2001 and the application for setting aside the ex parte decree was filed on 17.7.2001 within 10 days from the date of passing of the ex parte decree. In the application the defendant-opposite parties stated that 28.6.2001 was the date pre-ceding to the date of the ex parte decree but as the clerk of their learned Advocate supplied them an incorrect date, their caretaker did not appear in court on that date and as a result, they had no knowledge about the next date which was fixed on 7.7.2001. The opposite parties have explained in their application the reason for which they failed to take step on 5.7.2001 and as soon as, they came to know about the ex parte decree, they filed the application within 10 days from the date of the ex parte decree. The expression "prevented by sufficient cause" used in Rule 13 of Order 9 C.P.C. must be construed liberally to enable the court to exercise powers ex-debito justitiae. The failure of the learned Advocate to inform the correct date of hearing to the defendants, in my view, constitutes sufficient cause. 

6. In this case, the suit was decreed ex parte in the midst of the hearing and the application for setting aside the ex parte decree was made without any delay which itself is a good ground for setting aside the ex parte decree. The learned Assistant Judge, in the premises, is competent to come to a decision on the question of "sufficient cause" on affidavit evidence. Considering this aspect of the matter, the learned Assistant Judge has legally allowed the application without examining any witness subject to payment of Tk. 600/- as a condition precedent for setting aside the ex parte decree.

 In the view of the matter, I find no illegality or impropriety in the order of the learned Assistant Judge in setting aside the ex parte decree which calls for no interference by this court. This application merits no consideration which is rejected summarily. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, J : These two rules are directed against the judgment and decree dated 28.9.1983 (decrees signed on 1.11.86) passed in Other Appeal Nos. 2 of 1986 and 3 of 1986, heard and disposed of analogously by the District Judge, Chittagong on affirming the judgments and decrees dated 16.11.85 (decrees signed on 30.11.85) passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Other Suit Nos. 49 of 1976, 130 of 1976 and 87 of 1979 whereby Other Suit Nos. 49 of 76 and 130 of 76 were decreed and Other Suit No. 87 of 79 was dismissed on contest.

2. No one appears to support the rules.

3. These rules have been pending for disposal for over 16 years and the all further proceedings of the relevant execution cases have remained stayed over a decade. I am, therefore, inclined to take up these rules for disposal on merit on the basis of the materials on record.

4. Mr. Bhishna Dev Chakroborty, the learned Advocate appearing for the plain-tiff-opposite party, supports the impugned judgments.

5. The case of the plaintiff-opposite party is that the suit land recorded in R.S. Plot No. 358 of Mouza Ander Killa, P.S. Kotwali, District-Chittagong belonged to the plaintiff Deity and it has been correctly recorded in his name in the R.S. and P.S. khatians as a pond-Exts. 1 and 1(A) respectively. The suit land is a pond and its banks. The plaintiff has been owning and possessing the same in his own right, till he was dispossessed from a part of the suit land by the contesting defendant in 1970, which necessitated the filing of Other Suit No. 99 of 1970, re-numbered as Other Suit No. 130 of 1976 and Other Suit No. 49 of 197 respectively for declaration of tide and recovery of khas possession and for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land or, in the alternative, for recovery of khas possession therein. The case of the plaintiff Deity in Other Suit No. 49 of 1976 is that taking advantage of the abnormal situation prevailing in the country during the war of liberation the contesting defendant illegally filled up the said pond and eventually dispossessed the plaintiff completely on creating fraudulent and fake kabalas from one Gita Rani, although the alleged vendor had no title and possession in the suit land. In Other Suit No. 87 of 1979 the case of the plaintiff-petitioner was for a declaration that the proceedings of Misc. Case No. 159 of 1972 of the Court of the S.D.O (North) Chittagong and the orders passed therein on 23.2.72 and 4.3.72 directing him to deliver possession of the suit land in R.S. Plot No. 358 to the plain-tiff-opposite party are illegal and void and also for permanent injunction.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge heard the aforesaid there suits analogously and by his judgment dated 16.11.85 decreed Other Suit No. 49 of 76 and Other Suit No. 130 of 76 and dismissed Louver Suit No. 87 of 79 on contest against the present petitioners.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgments and decrees dated 16.1.85 (decrees signed on 30.11.85) passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, the present petitioners took two appeals before the District Judge, Chittagong being Other Appeal Nos. 2 of 86 and 3 of 86. It may be mentioned here in this connection that the present petitioners did not prefer any appeal against the dismissal of their Other Suit No. 87 of 1979, as the result of which the decision of Misc. Case No. 159 of 1972 by the S.D.O. (North), Chittagong remains binding upon the present petitioners.

8. The learned District Judge. Chittagong heard Other Appeal Nos. 2 of 1986 and 3 of 1986 analogously and dis-missed both the appeals by the impugned judgment dated 28.9.83, on affirming the impugned judgments and decrees passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong.

9. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgments and decrees dated 28.9.83, Osi Meah Sawdagor, the predecessor-in-interest of the present petitioners, moved this Court and obtained the present rules.

10. In view of the fact that the two rules arise out of the same judgment, I am inclined to dispose of these rules by a single judgment, as similar questions of law and facts are involved in the rules.

11. I have carefully gone through the impugned judgments passed by the learned Courts below and scrutinized the material evidence on record, both ocular and documentary. The only point for determination in the rules for me now is to see whether the learned District Judge committed any error of law occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgments.

12. On careful scrutiny of the impugned judgment passed by the learned District Judge, it is found that the learned District Judge took great pains in elaborately discussing and scrutinizing the facts and circumstances of the case, the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, and the law bearing on the subject and passed the impugned judgment with reference to the material evidence on record. The learned District Judge, as the final Court of fact, on proper assessment of the evidence on record, clearly found that the plaintiff has title in the suit property, from which the contesting defendant illegally dispossessed him around 1970, for which the plaintiff was constrained to file two suits seeking appropriate reliefs. It is found that the learned District Judge elaborately discussed and considered the respective cases of the contending parties and recorded clear findings on all material issues, with reference to the evidence on record.

13. The case of the defendant-petitioner is that the plaintiff of Other Suit No. 49 of 1976 and Other Suit No. 130 of 1976 settled the suit land with Raimohan and Harimohan by a patta dated 28.7.1933, the certified copy of which has been marked as Ext. B (1). Thereafter one Jogo Maya purchased the major portion of the interest of Raimohan and Harimohan by kabala dated 25.8.1948 in respect of Plot No. 360 and took settlement of the entire land of R.S. Plot No. 358. Subsequently by filling up the major portion of suit Plot of No. 358, Joga Maya constructed huts thereon. On her death the suit property devolved upon her daughter Gita Rani, who subsequently sold the land of R.S. Plot No. 360 to the defendant petitioner by a kabala dated 27.1.1970 and contracted to sell the remaining portion of the suit land to him by agreement dated 30.1.1970, at a consideration of Tk. 22,000.00, out of which Tk. 8,000.00 was paid as earnest money at the time of the contract. It has been alleged that subsequently he paid a further sum of Tk. 6,000.00 to Gita Rani on 25.3.1970 towards the consideration but the latter failed to execute and register the promised sale deed, following which the petitioner filed Title Suit No. 24 of 1971 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for specific performance of the contract and ultimately obtained an exported decree therein and got a kabala in respect of the suit property executed and registered through the Court. The contesting defendant further contended that he had to file Other Suit No. 87 of 1978 challenging the proceedings of Misc. Case No. 159 of 1972 in the Court of S.D.O. (North). Chittagong for undoing its orders for making over vacant possession of the suit land to the plaintiff.

14. In this case there is no dispute to the fact that the case land was a pond and it belonged to the plaintiff and it was recorded correctly as a pond in the name of the plaintiff in the R.S. and B.S. kalians. The plain case of the defendant-petitioner is that the plaintiff, being in-rightful possession of the same, settled it with Raimohan and Harimohan who subsequently sold a portion of the suit land to Joga Maya by kabala dated 25.8.1948. It has been also asserted that, in course of time, the pond silted up, following which Joga Maya constructed huts therein and on Joga Maya's death, her daughter Gita Rani inherited the same and sold out the homestead to the contesting defendant by kabala dated 27.1.1970 and contracted to sell the suit land to the contesting defendant by an agreement dated 30.7.1970 at a consideration of Tk. 22,000.00. It has been alleged that, in course of time, the defendant petitioner filed Title Suit No. 74 of 1971 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong and obtained a kabala through Court and since then he has been owning and possessing the same. It has also been pleaded by the defendant petitioner that Joga Maya and Gila Rani perfected their title in the suit land by way of adverse possession and as such the plain-tiff was left with no title and interest in the suit land. Evidently the anchor sheet of the case of the contesting defendant is the kabala-dated 25.8.1948 executed by Raimohan and Harimohan in favour of Joga Maya and subsequently the decree obtained by him in Title Suit No. 24 of 1971. The learned District Judge on thorough discussion and consideration of the evidence on record found that the contesting defendant petitioner has failed to adduce any acceptable evidence to prove that Joga Maya and her daughter Gita Rani acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession. The learned District Judge clearly found that D.W. 2, who came to prove the possession of the defendant in the suit land, is a hired witness and he has practically to knowledge about the suit land. Admittedly the suit land is situated in the heart of the city of Chittagong but not a single neighboring person has been examined by the defendant to prove his claim that Joga Maya and Gita Rani had actual physical possession on in the suit land for twelve years, on denying the plaintiffs title therein so as to constitute adverse possession in their favour. There is also no evidence to prove that the plaintiff had no possession in the suit land till before he was dispossessed therefrom by the contesting defendant in 1970-71. It is the case of the defendant-petitioner that he purchased the suit land from Gita Rani with structures standing thereon. This kabala has been marked as Ext. A(1), which clearly shows that Plot No. 360 and not suit Plot No. 358 was sold to the defendant-petitioner by this kabala Ext. A(1). The petitioner's kabala Ext. A(1) clearly mentions that suit plot No. 358 was a pond and not a dwelling house at the time of the kabala, as claimed by him. This basic document of the defendant petitioner Ext. A(1) thus falsifies, beyond redemption, the petitioner's case that the suit pond had earlier silted up. following which his predecessor in-interest Gita Rani and her mother Joga Maya possessed it by constructing huts thereon. The learned District Judge, on elaborate discussion of the evidence, clearly found that the story of adverse possession by Joga Maya and Gita Rani has not been proved at all. Patta dated 28.7.1933 marked as Ext. B executed by the plaintiff in favour of Raimohan and Harimohan clearly shows that these two men were given only a limited right to use the water of the pond and its bank and nothing more. It is evident that Raimohan and Harimohan were at best given a limited right of use of the water of the pond and its bank, while the plaintiff opposite party continued to be the ostensible owner-in-possession thereof. There is absolutely no evidence on record to find that with the lapse of time Raimohan and Harimohan ever denied the title of the plaintiff in the suit land by asserting hostile title in the pond and its bank. The learned District Judge found, with reference to the evidence, that the little easement right which Raimohan and Harimohan might have enjoyed for themselves and for their heirs and heiresses evaporated with the sealing up of the pond and it could never go to any outsider claiming through them, it being specifically confined to the members of the family.

<u>15. Section 44 of the Easement Act provides that an easement is extinguished where the sentient heritage or the subject-matter of the easement is so permanently altered that the dominant owner can no longer enjoy the easement. In the instant case, it is the specific case of the contesting defendant that with the lapse of time, the suit pond fully silted up and permanently changed its character as a pond, following which the contesting defendants processors-in-interest Gita Rani and her mother Joga Maya constructed dwelling huts thereon. Subsequently the defendant purchased it from Gita Rani with structures standing thereon. In the facts of the case and the evidence of record, it stands proved beyond doubt that the pond in question has so permanently changed its character that the alleged dominant owner can no long enjoy the easement. It is thus crystal clear that the alleged easement right of the contesting defendant in the suit property totally extinguished, by sub-sequent developments by a total change of the nature and character of the property. As a matter of fact, no right of easement in the suit property could be proved by the contesting defendant by adducing any evidence worthy of credence. The story of having an easement right in the suit property stands out as a sheer myth.</u>

16. The learned District Judge, as the final Court of the fact, also clearly found that the plaintiff convincingly proved that he has title in the suit land, from which the contesting defendant-petitioner illegally dispossessed him in 1970-71. Admittedly the pond silted up around 1970 and with that the alleged easement right completely extinguished and the land reverted to the plaintiff as its undisputed owner. So, by purchase of the suit land by the contesting defendant from Gita Rani by kabala dated 27.1.1970 and by obtaining decree in Other Suit No. 24 of 1971, the defendant acquired to right, title and interest in the suit land. These findings of facts arrived at by the learned Court of appeal below are well-supported by convincing oral and documentary evidence. The 3 P.Ws. examined by the plain-tiff uniformly and consistently stated in their evidence that the contesting defendant entered in a portion of the suit land in 1970 and thereafter forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff from the remaining portion of the suit land in 1971 and constructed huts thereon. Both the learned District Judge and the learned Subordinate Judge concurrently found that the defendant totally failed to prove that his predecessors-in-interest, namely Gita Rani and Joga Maya or Raimohan and Harimohan had acquired any title in the suit land so as to pass title to the defendant-petitioner. It is also found from the patta dated 28.7.1933 Ext. B(1) that Raimohan and Harimohan settled R.S. Plot No. 358 with Joga Maya, al bait, with no title, for a period of 9 years only and allowed her to use the water of the pond and its bank for the same period. The learned Courts below also concurrently found that there is no evidence on record to prove that Joga Maya or Gita Rani ever claimed title in the suit land at any relevant time. I find no evidence on record to hold that Joga Maya continued to possess the suit land after the expiry of the period of the mortgage for 9 years. On elaborate discussion of the evidence, both oral and documentary, the learned Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff has successfully proved his title and possession in the suit land till before he was forcibly dispossessed by the contesting defendant therefrom in 1970-71. It must, therefore, be held that the learned Courts below rightly found that the suit is not barred by limitation or by adverse possession. These material findings of fact are found to be well-reasoned and well-sup-ported by the evidence on record. The learned District Judge as well as the learned Subordinate Judge duly applied their judicial mind into the material evidence and the material documents of the defendant, viz Ext. A(1), Exts. B and B(1) on which the defendant relies, and discarded these documents on assigning convincing reasons. The impugned judgment is thus found to be concluded by concurrent findings of fact, which are fully sup-ported by proper appreciation of the evidence on record. The grievances of the petitioner that his basic documents have not been duly considered and correctly construed are found to be totally baseless and unsubstantiated. I have carefully scrutinized the material Exts of the case - and I find that the learned Courts below were fully justified in decreeing the suits on proper appreciation of the material evidence and right construction of the exhibited documents of the contending parties. I do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment occasioning failure of justice so as to justify interference by this Court exercising revisional power under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, I, therefore, find no merit in the rules which must fail accordingly.

17. In the result, the two rules are discharged without any order as to cost and the impugned judgments and decrees dated 28.9.1983 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 2 of 1986 and Other Appeal No. 3 of 1986, on affirming the judgments and decrees 16.11.1985 passed by the learned 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 49 of 1976 and Other Suit No. 130 of 1976 decreeing the suits, are affirmed.

18. The order staying all further proceedings of Other Execution Case No. 22 of 1985 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong and further proceedings of Other Execution Case No. 23 of 1985 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, pending hearing of the rules, is vacated.

19. The learned Execution Court is hereby directed to dispose of the execution cases with utmost expediency, preferably within 3 months from the date of receipt of this order.

20. Communicate the order at once to the learned 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for his information and necessary action.

21. Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, J: Feeling aggrieved by judgment and order dated 19.9. 1993 recorded by learned Subordinate Judge, First Court. Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 under Order-41, Rule-21 and Section-151 of the Code of Civil Procedure dismissing miscellaneous case appellant approached this Court in this First Miscellaneous Appeal.

	2. Appellant is defendant No. 2 in the suit and Respondent in the Title appeal. Predecessors of Respondent Nos. 1-9 had been plaintiffs in the suit and appellant in the appeal. Respondent No. 10 is defendant No. 1 and Respondent No. 1 in the suit and appeal respectively. 

	3. A resume of facts and events leading to this appeal may be set out in brief. 

	4. Predecessor of respondent Nos. 1-9 as plaintiff laid a suit being Title Suit No. 667 of 1977 in Second Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge). Barisal Sadar for a decree of recovery of khas possession on Ka-schedule property described in the plaint on evicting defendants therefrom. 

	5. Respondent No. 10 as defendant No. 1 contested the suit on presentation of a written statement. Appellant as defendant No. 2 did neither enter appearance nor did contest the suit. 

	The said suit was dismissed by judgment and decree dated 24.2.1980 by learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Barisal. 

	6. Plaintiffs carried an appeal being Title Appeal No. 73 011980 before learned District Judge, Barisal. Learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal heard the appeal and by judgment and decree dated 29.3.1984 allowed the appeal set aside the judgment and decree recorded by trial judge and decreed the suit on contest against defendant respondent Nos. 1 and 2. 

	7. Appellant (defendant No. 2-Respondent No. 2) as petitioner, thereafter laid an application being numbered Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rehearing of the appeal taking grounds that appellant had been Respondent No. 2 in appeal and no summons or notices had been at all served upon her and those were fraudulently suppressed by plaintiff-respondent in collusion with process server and appellant resided at Chittagong with her husband and at the time of alleged service of summons she was at Chittagong and she was not at all aware of the institution of Title Suit as well as of appeal. Further contention was that husband of Respondent No. 10 had not been her agent and as such he had no authority to accept the summons on her behalf. She for the first time became aware of the appeal matter from Kamal, son of Abdul Goni on 4.5.1984 and through her Advocate clerk on 7.4.1984 became fully aware of appeal matter. 

	8. Respondent Nos. 1-9 resisted the Miscellaneous Case on presentation of a written objection taking stand that Miscellaneous Case stood barred by limitation and appellant did not reside at Chittagong. Assertion made was that she was fully aware of proceeding of appeal but defaulted in appearing. Further pleading was that husband of Respondent No. 10 was her agent. 

	9. Evidence had been led in support of the respective contentions of the contending parties. 

	10. Learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal by impugned judgment and order dated 19.9.1993 rejected Miscellaneous Case. In recording rejection learned Subordinate Judge took the view that Miscellaneous Case was filed after a period of one month and twelve days and the case stood barred by limitation. Learned Judge also found that Shorup Ali, vital witness for appellant was not examined. Learned Judge also discarded the testimony of P.W.3 on ground of relationship with appellant Learned Judge also took the view that without moving to Higher Court against judgment and decree recorded in appeal appellant filed Miscellaneous Case under Order 41, Rule-21 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Miscellaneous Case is not maintainable. Learned Judge, thereafter, took the view that appeal was allowed on contest against Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and appellant was respondent No. 2 in appeal and as such Miscellaneous Case under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure was untenable. Learned Judge, thereafter, found that appellant failed to substantiate her case through competent. independent and trustworthy witnesses. 

	11. The vires of judgment and order under appeal had been challenged in raising manifold contentions from the side of appellant. 

	12. Mr. Zakir Hossain Munshi, learned Advocate appeared for appellant. Respondents are represented by Mr. F.R.M. Nazmui Ahsan, learned Advocate. 

	13. The first branch of contention advanced from the side of appellant is that decree of the appeal had been drawn on 3.5.1984 and Miscellaneous Case under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been filed on 10.5.1984 and as such Miscellaneous Case was not at all barred by limitation and learned Subordinate Judge committed a substantial error in holding that Miscellaneous case was barred by limitation. 

	14. In order to appreciate the said contention provision contained in Article 169 of the Limitation Act may conveniently be noticed. 

	15. Article 169 of the Limitation Act runs thus: 

	“The date of the decree in appeal, or, where notice of the appeal was not duly served, when the applicant has knowledge of the decree." 

	16. Article 169 enshrines that for rehearing of an appeal ex parte an application can be filed within 30 days from the date of the decree in a case notice is duly served and from the date of knowledge of the decree if notice is not duly served. 

	17. Miscellaneous case was very much within 30 days of the date of the decree in appeal and as such it cannot be at all said that miscellaneous case stood barred by limitation as held by learned Subordinate Judge. The first branch of contention got a substance. 

	18. Provision contained in Rule-21 of Order 41 may also profitably be seen. Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code read thus:-

	"21. where an appeal is heard ex parte and judgment is pronounced against the respondent, he may apply to the Appellate Court to re-hear the appeal; and, if he satisfies the Court that the notice was not duly served or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the appeal was called on for hearing, the Court shall re-hear the appeal on such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit to impose upon him." 

	19. Order 41, Rule 21 provides that when an appeal is heard ex parte and judgment is pronounced as against the respondent, he may apply to the Appellate Court to re-hear the appeal and if he satisfies the Court that the notice was not duly served or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the appeal was called on for hearing, the Court shall re-hear the appeal on such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit to impose upon them. 

	20. From the plaint of Title Suit No. 667 of 1977 it appears that address of defendant No. 2 appellant was not at all given. From the Report of Process server it appears that address of defendant No. 2 appellant had not been even stated. Summons upon her was alleged to have been caused upon defendant No. 4 Zakia Begum showing her as agent of defendant No. 2 appellant and she having refused to accept summon said was alleged to have been served on hanging on the door of the house. In Memorandum of appeal defendant No. 2-respondent No. 2 appellant had been shown as Principal respondent No. 2 and she was shown to be resident of Nazir Mohalla and in the summons of the appeal her address was not even given. In the service return Process Server reported that defendant-respondent No. 2 having been at Chittagong was not available and notice was tendered to Respondent No. 1 and her husband and they accepted notices. 

	21. In Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure Respondent No. 2 appellant's address had been stated to be C.G.O. Colony Agrabad, Chittagong. In written objection filed for and on behalf of Respondents there is no assertion that appellant did never stay at Chittagong and always resided at Nazir Mohalla, Barisal. It is not understood how address of appellant having not been given in the plaint, Memorandum of appeal as well as in summons, summons could be served upon her. Appellant as P.W.1 in Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 testified that she was not served summons and notice of appeal and she became aware of ex parte judgment recorded in appeal on 4.5.1984 from her nephew and, thereafter, came to Barisal and came to know on 7.5.1984 that appeal was allowed and decree was recorded against her. Testimony of appellant as P.W.1 could not be shattered through grueling cross-examination from the side of respondents. P.W.3 gave testimony that on 4.5.1984 he informed her Mami i.e. P.W.1 at her Chittagong residence that other party obtained ex parte decree. The testimony of this witness also could not be shaken by way of any cross-examination from the side of respondents. From testimonies the appellant could successfully substantiate her case that on 4.5.1984 she became aware of the ex parte decree in the appeal against her. It had already been found that miscellaneous case was not barred by limitation and the same was filed within stipulated period and knowledge of ex parte decree also could be substantiated. Learned Subordinate Judge, thus, fell into a substantiate error in holding that Miscellaneous case was barred by limitation and appellant could not prove her case through competent, independent and trustworthy witnesses. The ground canvassed by learned Subordinate Judge in discarding the case of appellant that P.Ws.1 and 2 were relations and P.W.3 is an interested witness and testimony of P.W.3 was not reliable not at all tenable one inasmuch as testimony of a relation cannot be blown away simply on the ground that he or she is related with a party and the value of the testimony can be demolished only if it is characterized by internal marks of falsehood. 

	22. This takes me to another aspect of the matter. From service return of Process Server in the appeal there is endorsement by Process Server that appellant stayed at Chittagong and service was alleged to have been caused upon Respondent No. 1 and her husband showing them as her agents. From service return it becomes manifestly clear that she stayed at the relevant time at Chittagong and so service on her at Nazir Mohalla, Barisal instead of Chittagong is no service in the eye of law. 

	23. Law is well settled that an agent must be authorised by a person on whose behalf he is authorised to act and that agentnama must be is writing. No document had been produced from the side of respondents that respondent No.1 and her husband are authorised agents or got any agentnama in writing to receive any summon or notice for and on behalf of appellant. 

	24. Contention was pressed into service from the side of appellant that she did never enter appearance in appeal and appeal was heard and disposed of ex parte against her and learned Subordinate Judge committed a manifest error in holding that appeal was decided on contest against her and Miscellaneous case under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure was untenable. 

	25. On a careful examination of record of appeal it does not at all appear that Respondent No. 2 appellant did even enter any appearance by any Vokalatnama or in any other way. The decision rendered by learned Subordinate Judge that appeal stood allowed on contest against respondent No. 2 suffers from patent illegality perversity and flagrant error of law. Learned Subordinate Judge did not at all apply his mind and did not also examine record. This type of carelessness on the part of a Subordinate Judge is unfortunate. 

	26. Since the appeal was heard and disposed of ex parte against respondent No. 2 appellant miscellaneous case under Order 41, Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure was very much maintainable. 

	27. Having considered facts and circumstances and pros and cons of the whole matter I am of this considered view that judgment and order recorded by learned Subordinate Judge dated 19.9.1993 should be quashed and Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 be allowed and appeal be reheard. 

	28. Resultantly, this First Miscellaneous Appeal is allowed. Judgment and order dated 19.9.1993 recorded by learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal stand set aside. Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1984 is allowed and Title Appeal No. 73 of 1980 be heard. 

	29. Since the Civil proceeding commenced in the year 1977 and long 23 years had already passed justice demands that appeal be disposed of as expeditious as possible and for that a direction is recorded hereunder. 

	29. Learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal is directed to hear and dispose of Title Appeal No. 73 of 1980 within 3 (three) months positively from the date of receipt of the judgment and records. The appellant in this appeal and respondent No. 2 in Title Appeal No. 73 of 1980 will appear in the appeal within one month of the arrival of the record in appellate court. In default, the appeal will be heard and disposed of ex parte. 

	30. The order of stay staying proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1993 pending in the Court will continue during pendency of the appeal. 

	31. Regard being had to the fact and circumstances of the case I direct th:t parties to bear their respective costs of the litigation. 

	32. Send down the L.C.R. immediately.
End.
