full_judgment:
Mr. Abdus Salam Mainun J: The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment Order dated 30.04.2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Appeal No.5 of 1995 reversing the Order dated 8.1.1955 passed by No.7 Eozbalia Gram Adalat, Sadar, Noakhali, in Case No.195 of 1994 should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Petitioner made an application to No.7 Eozbalia Union Gram Adalat for realization of compensation of Taka 4,000/- from the opposite party on the grounds stated therein. The same was registered as Grama Adalat Case No.195 of 1994. On 8.1.95 the said Gram Adalat passed their unanimous judgment by the three members decreeing the case. The opposite party then preferred a Miscellaneous Appeal being No.5 of 1995 before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali and the learned Senior Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment and Order dated 30.4.2001 has been pleased to reverse the judgment and decree passed by the Gram Adalat. As against the Judgment and Order the petitioner has moved this Hon'ble Court and obtained the instant Rule. 3. Mr. A.K.M. Abdul Malek, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that under the Village Courts Ordinance, 1976 the learned Senior Assistant Judge was not competent to entertain an appeal to decide merit of the case and further that the said appeal was hopelessly time barred. 

4. No one appeared for the opposite party. 

5. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner, perused the application together with annexures and impugned Judgment and Order and it appears that the Gram Adalat in their Order dated 8. i .95 found that the petitioner was the owner, possessor and person-in-interest of the land in question by inheritance and the opposite party on 24.11.1994 has trespassed into the land of the petitioner, took away earth by cutting and filed in some part of the land and also attempted to construct a thatched house with the help of some others and as such, the petitioner was being under threat of his life and reputation lodged the Complaint on 24.12.94. The opposite party received the process of the Adalat directing him to maintain status quo but in defiance of he Order of the Adalat the opposite party has constructed a thatched house taken away and filled earth and thus caused loss to the petitioner to the tune of Taka 4,000/, The Grameen Adalat has therefore decreed compensation for an amount of Taka 4,000b and awarded fine of Taka 300/- against the opposite party for committing contempt of the Adalat and directed to the opposite party to pay the same within 8.2.95 and to remove the thatched house within the period. The opposite party thereafter has preferred the said Miscellaneous Appeal before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Noakhali who took up the matter for judgment on 30.4. 2001 and observed that the Village Court had restrained the opposite party by way of injunction from entering into the land and constructing house, as apparent from the judgment itself which was not within its jurisdiction and also that in the impugned judgment the Adalat has directed the opposite party to remove the thatched house within 8.2.1995 which is otherwise a decree for eviction and not within the jurisdiction of the Village Court. The learned Assistant Judge also found that the Gram Adalat did not elaborate in its Judgment the mischief and other losses for which it had awarded that compensation for an amount of Tk.4000.00. The learned Assistant Judge therefore has been pleased to allow the Miscellaneous Appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Village Court on 8.1.95 in Village Court Case No.195 of 1994. 

6. A Village Court is constituted under the Village' Court Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance No. LXI of 1976) having jurisdictions under Section 3 to try all Cases and Suits mentioned in the schedule notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure or in the code of Civil Procedure and also having Jurisdiction to Order the accused to pay to the aggrieved person compensation under Section 7 of an amount not exceeding Taka 5,000/- if it holds a person guilty of an offence specified in part 1 of the Schedule and under Section 8, if the decision of the Village Court, is unanimous or by a majority of four to one, the decision shall be binding on the parties and be enforceable in accordance with the provisions on the Ordinance. Sub-section (2) of Section 8 provides that if the decision of a Village Court is by a majority of three to two, any party may, within thirty days of the decision, apply, in the prescribed manner-(a) to the Sub divisional Magistrate (now upazila Magistrate) if the case relates to an offence specified in Part 1 of the Schedule, and (d) to the Munsif (now Assistant Judge) if the case relates to a matter specified in Part 11 of the Schedule and if the Sub divisional Magistrate or the Munsif is satisfied that there has been a failure of justice, may aside or modify the decision, or direct that the dispute be referred back to the Village Court for reconsideration. Under Section 11 of the Ordinance a Village Court, under certain circumstances, may hold a person guilty of contempt and may take appropriate actions provided under the Section. The Section reads as follows: 
"11. Contempt of Village Courts. —A person shall be guilty of contempt of a Village Court if he, without lawful excuse,- 
a. offers any insult to the Court or any member thereof while the Court is functioning as such; or b. causes any interruption in the work of The Court: or 
c. fails to produce or deliver a document when ordered by the Court to do so; or 
d. refuse to answer any question of the Court which he is bound to answer; or 
e. refuse to take oath to state the truth or to sign any statement made by him when required by he Court to do so; and the Court may, without, any complaint having been made to it, forthwith try such person for such contempt and sentence him to a fine not exceeding five hundred Taka. 

7. In the instant case, the decision of the Village Court was made on 8.1.95 and the appeal was preferred on 29.7.95. Under Section 8(2) of the Village Court Ordinance, 1976 the time limitation to apply to the Magistrate or Assistant Judge is 30(thirty) days from the date of decision. The learned Assistant Judge in. his impugned Judgment and Order dated 30.4.2001 has nowhere took up this point of limitation for discussion nor has he stated anything as to whether the limitation was condoned. Time limitation was being the preliminary point on the maintainability of the appeal the learned Assistant Judge ought to have given his reason at the outset. Section 8(2) provides that if the decision of a Village Court is by a majority of three to two, in that case only any party may apply to the Sub-divisional Magistrate or the Munsif, as the case may be. But Section 8(1) provides that if the decision of a Village Court, is unanimous or by a majority of four to one, the decision shall be binding on the parties and shall be enforceable with the provisions of the Ordinance. In the instant case, the decision was given unanimously by all the three members of the Adalat and as such, no petition was maintainable to the Munsif sub-section (1) of Section 8 of the Ordinance. On the other hand, the matters relate to offences of trespass, theft and mischief are under part I of the Schedule and not under part 11 of the same and since the learned Munsif has been given jurisdiction only in respect of part 1 I and not in respect of part I, the impugned order was therefore without jurisdiction. 

8. The Gram Adalat is found to have been constituted in accordance with Section 5 and acted within their jurisdiction and no interference was called for from the learned Munsif under the given facts and circumstances. Order for maintaining status quo during the pendency of the Petition before the Adalat for decision and an Order for removal of any structure made in defiance of the Order in not beyond the Jurisdiction of the Adalat. 

9. In the result; the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 30.04.2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Appeal No.5 of 1995 is hereby set aside. Send down the L.C. Records at once. Communicate. 
End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Khondker Musa Khaled, J : This Rule, arising out of an application under section 115(1) of the code of civil procedure is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 03.02.2000 passed by the learned District Judge, Madaripur, in title appeal no. 13 of 1999 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 14.02.1999 passed by the learned senior Assistant Judge, rajoir, Madaripur, in title suit no. 27 of1995 rejecting the plaint under order 7 rule 11(d) of the code of civil procedure. 

2. The relevant facts, necessary for disposal of the rule, are that the petitioners predecessor Adam All Howlader filed the above noted suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land as the defendant 4 started claiming interest in the same on the basis of settlement from the O.P. I (Government) who alleged to have acquired title to the suit land by auction sale held in certificate case No. 1571 M. 1/67-68 due to areas rents. Previously, the plaintiff Adam Ali Howlader filed another suit bearing no. 219 of 1972 in. the Court of Assistant Judge, Madaripur, for declaration that the auction sale dated 16.06.1969 and lease deed of the defendant 4 from the auction purchaser were illegal and void, and the suit was decreed on 21.08.1978. But it was set aside on appeal and the suit was sent back on remand to the trial court for holding trial of the suit afresh. Thereafter, on the advice of the well wisheres, the opposite party 4 (defendant 4) executed a deed of relinquishment in favour of Adam Ali Howlader (predecessor of the petitioners) on 24.03.1973. But concealing the compromise, the suit was allowed to he dismissed on 28.01.1978 and the defendant 4 (opposite party 4) started claiming the suit property during Buzarat proceeding. So the predecessor of the present plaintiff namely Adam All Howlader instituted this suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the same suit land. 

3. The defendant no. 4 contested the suit by filing written statement and on the basis of the pleaings, issues were framed and thereafter the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing. One of. the witness of the petitioner had also been examined partly. At that stage the defendant 4 (opposite party 4) submitted an application on 02.02.1998 under order 7 rule 11(d) of the code of civil procedure for rejection of the plaint stating that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata as the previously instituted title suit no. 219 of 1972 was dismissed on contest on 28.01.1978 resolving the same disputed issues involved in the present suit. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge allowed the petition and rejected the plaint by his judgment dated 03.02.2000 holding the view that the suit was barred by resjudicata under section 11 of the code of Civil Procedure. On appeal, the learned District Judge also held the same view. Hence the plaintiff petitioner preferred the present revisional application against the judgment and decree passed by the courts below.

5. Mr. Md Khalilur Rahmn, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the decision on the issue of res judicata can not be decided without taking evidence and taking decisions in other issues involved in the suit. According to his contention the rejection of the plaint on the ground of res judicata at the stage of peremptory hearing of the suit is bad in law. It is submitted that the courts below have committed mistake in coming to the conclusion that the issues of the previous suit and those of the present one are same without looking to the facts and circumstances leading to the filling of the present suit. He submits that the question of re judicata, being a mixed question of law and fact, is not a matter to be decided on the basis of an application for rejection of the plaint rather it requires adjudication at the time of final hearing of the 'suit on the basis of evidence to be adduced by the parties. It is submitted that fraud was practiced by the defendant 4 in getting the prior suit dismissed without submitting compromise petition. The subsequent nadabi patra executed by the defendant 4 is also a matter to be decided at the time of trial. So, the decision on the rejection of the plaint on the ground or res judicata is not available from the mere reading of the plaint rather it requires adjudication. 

6. Mr. Mohammad Qzair Farooq, the learned senior Advocate, assisted by his junior Mr. A.K.M. Salimullah, appearing on behalf of the opposite party 4, submits that the prior suit of the petitioners predecessor Adam Ali Howlader was filed challenging validity of the certificate sale proceeding and the said suit was admittedly dismissed on contest. Since no appeal was preferred, the same question. as to the validity of the auction sale can not be reaqitated in the present suit, As such, the learned courts below have rightly decided the question taking concurrent view that the present suit is barred by res judicata and as such the plaint is liable to be rejected. It is also contended that the plaintiff, having been failed to prefer an appeal from the judgment and decree of the prior suit and seek specific relief against the previous decree in the form of declaration imputing its validity, the plaintiffs subsequent suit can not be maintainable as stands barred by the law of resjudicata. 

7. On hearing submission of the learner Advocate and perusal of the case records, i appears from the plaint of the present suit that Adam Ali Howlader claimed ownership of .7 acres of land recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 59 in the names of two brothers Bashiram Mondal and Radhanath Mondal stating that on the death of Radhanath Mondals, the suit land devolve, on his brother Bashiram who also died leaving the only daughter in Shushila Bala Shikder, and the plaintiffs predecessor Adam Ali Howlader Purchased the suit land from the said Shushila bala Shikder by a registered Kobala dated 03.01.1970. But the suit land was shown to have been auction purchased by the, Government (Defendant-I) for arrear rents. The, Same plaintiff previously filed title suit no. 219 of 1972 challenging legality of the said auction sale and subsequent settlement to the defendant 4. The defendant 4 contested the suit on the assertion that he acquired interest in the sui land by taking settlement from the Government So, if the alleged auction sale is decided to be legal in the previous suit, the plaintiffs claim of title by purchase from the female heir of the S.A. recorded tenant does not stand. The question termination of prior tenancy right o the S.A. recorded tenants by the impugned auction is essentially a vital issue which is directly and sub sequentially in issue in both the suits filed by the same plaintiff against the same set of defendants in respect of the same land. 

8. It appears from the certified copy of the judgment passed in title suit no. 219 of 197 that the learned Munsif, who previously decree the suit and later on dismissed it on getting the suit on remand, found that the certificate case was proceeded legally and that the plaintiff having no locus standi to file the suit until hi title is established is not entitled to get an relief in that suit. It is evident that the plaintil and the defendant filed solenama in the previous suit on 08.03.1977 and thereafter the plaintiff remained absent at the time of rehearing of the suit after remand. Though the said solenama filed by the plaintiff and the defendant 2 of that suit (Plaintiff and defendant 4 in the present suit, was rejected at the time of i pronouncement of the judgment, the recital of the said solenama was taken into consideration by the learned Assistant Judge to base his findings and decision of the suit on merit, which was not at all legal and proper. 

9. The plaintiff of the present suit has alleged in para 4(kha) of the plaint that the defendant 4 fraudulently and collusively obtained the decree in the previous suit beyond his knowledge by concealing the original compromise petition executed by the parties and if the said compromise petitioners was filed, the prior suit ought to have been decreed on compromise. Since the plaintiff relied upon the defendant 4 in good faith in the matter of submitting the compromise petition, and remained absent the defendant 4 was able to get the suit dismissed in a fraudulent manner, which was passed in the absence of the plaintiff, It is also stated in the plaint that subsequently the defendant 4 admitting his foul play in the matter, had executed a nadabi patra on 24.03.1978 relinquishing his claim on the suit property. So, this subsequent event on the matter of relinquishment of claim on the suit' land by the defendant 4 is required to be adjudicated for the purpose of ascertaining the present suit on the basis of nadabi patra which was subsequent to the decree. Further it is evident from the judgment passed in the previous suit that no decision was arrived at on the vital question of possession on the basis of evidence on record which is also necessary to be adjudicated in the present suit filed for a declaration of title and confirmation of possession. 

10. The learned Advocate for the opposite party no. 4 has pointed out that the averment of the plaint shows that the plaintiff was aware of the alleged fraudulent decree as early as early on 24.03.1978 when a nadabi patra was said to have been executed by the defendant 4 in 
favour of the plaintiff, As such the present suit filed in the year 1995 is also barred by limitation. However, the learned courts below did not also consider the point of limitation in the impugned judgment and decree. 

11. Thus it is clear that the result of the present suit is dependent on the proof of the asserted facts relating to fraud possession of the parties and adjudication on the question of limitation. Mixed questions of law and fact are involved in taking decision in the aforesaid matters, which can only be decided at the time of trial obviously after taking evidence. In the case of Md. Mahbubul Haque Vs. Md. Abdul Qader Munshi reported in 20 BLD(AD) 82, their lordships held question of res judicata can not be decided from reading of the plaint and should be decided at the time of trial. The same view was also taken in the case of Sreemoti Pushpo Rani Das Vs. A.K.M Habibur Rahman and others reported in 13 BLD(AD) 217. On the question of limitation also there is decision of our Apex Court to the effect that it can only be decided at the time of trial as the matter involves mixed question of law and fact. The decision was taken in the case of Mabhubuddin Vs. Habibur Rahman reported in 50 DLR (AD) 99. 

12. It appears that the present suit was fixed for peremptory hearing after framing of issues and deposition of P.W. 1 was also partly recorded. At that stage, the defendant 4 filed the application for rejecting the plaint under order 7 rule 11(d) of the code of civil procedure on the ground that the suit nos. barred by res judicata. It was not proper to reject the plaint at the stage of peremptory hearing of the suit leaving the other issues unanswered such matter is required to be taken up at the earliest stage of the suit it has been settled in the case reported in 13 BLD(AD) 217 that the plea of res judicata is not available in the matter of rejecting a plaint under order 7 rule 11 of the code of civil procedure. Because it requires adjudication of the pleadings of the parties by taking evidence and such matters can hardly be decided from the plaint reading of the plaint particularly when allegation of fraud in obtaining the prior decree had been made out in the plaint. It is a settled principle that ordinarily plaint should not be rejected on the ground of res judicata, unless it is so palpably clear from a reading of the plaint and no further evidence is necessary to substantiate the pleading. To be in the safe side. It is better to frame issue relating to res judicata alone, with other issues and decide the matter at the time of pronouncing final judgment. In the present case, when the issues have already been framed, other issues can not be left un attended for the purpose of effective and complete adjudication of the pleadings involved in the suit. The plaintiff petitioner, having alleged that fraud was practiced upon him as well as on the court by the defendant opposite party in obtaining the decree in the prior suit, the plaintiffs should not be non suited by rejecting plaint without considering other aspects. There is, however, substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party that the plaintiff in the present suit has not asked for any specific relief against the prior judgment and decree in the form of declaration that it was obtained by fraud and as such, it was illegal and void. I have already mentioned earlier that there are material facts in the plaint about practicing fraud in the matter of non submission of actual compromise petition in the previous suit and as such the suit was finally dismissed in the absence of the plaintiff. In view of the averments made out in the plaint, the plaintiffs may be permitted to seek further relief in the line of the fact narrated in the plaint by way of amendment for ends of justice. 

13. Having due regard to the aforesaid facts, circumstances and legal position, I am constrained to hold that both the courts before committed mistake in rejecting the plaint outright on the ground of res judicata without proper adjudication after taking evidence Disposal of the suit on the decision of res judicata issue without holding trial and without taking decision in other necessary issues involved in the suit, resulted erroneous decision which occasioned failure of justice. 

14. In the result the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The judgments an decrees of the courts below are set aside. The suit is sent back to the trial court on remand providing opportunity to get plaint amended seeking specific relief against the prior decree and thereafter to hold trial of the suit by taking evidence. The learned Assistant Judge is alsp directed to recast the issues framed earlier by inserting the issue of res judicata with other related matters in the suit on the basis or the pleadings of the parties as discussed above thereafter he shall proceed with the trial in accordance with law and in the light of bservations made out in the judgment. 

15. Send down the lower court records at once. 

End.

Mr. Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman, J: The supplementary affidavit dated 13.4.2004 do form part of the main writ petition. 

2. In this writ application the writ petitioner has challenged the order dated 20.3.2004 wherefrom it appear that the learned Judge heard two applications but the said order reflects that 
only the application filed by the Decree-holder on 13.11.2003 has been disposed of and no order has been passed on the application tiled by the Judgment-debtor on 27.1.2004 and that while disposing of the application of the Decree-holder the possession of the mortgaged property has been ordered to be delivered to the Decree-holder bank allowing it to enjoy usufructs therefrom and authorizing the Decree-holder bank to satisfy its decree by sale of the mortgaged property under Section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. 

3. Perused the application and heard the learned advocate. 

4. The learned Advocate appearing for the writ petitioner submits that as the application dated 27.01.04 filed by the Judgment-debtor or under Order 26, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been disposed of and in the mean-time the possession of the mortgaged property, which is now under possession of the Judgment-debtor, ordered to be delivered to the Decree-holder bank and that the Judgment debtor will be put to suffer irreparable injury if possession, as ordered for, is delivered inasmuch_ as the said property is the only homestead land of the writ petitioner and that subsequent to the passing of the decree, the judgment-debtor, on the passing of the decree, the Judgment debtor. on the assurance of the Decree-holder bank, has already deposited the cost of the suit plus 10% of the claimed amount with the Decree-holder Bank to get remission of the interest and that prayer is pending and that this fact has not been considered by the Court below and that the said amount as deposited, has not also been adjusted with the decretal amount and hence the judgment-debtor being aggrieved moved this application under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

5. It appears that the Judgment debtor wants adjustment of the aforesaid amount which they have deposited after passing of the decree, on the assurance of the Decree-holder bank to the effect that the interest amount will be remitted and that the said matter is still rending and is under consideration of the Bank. We are of the view that the executing Court can not look 
beyond the decree and if the claim of the Judgment debtor writ petitioner is correct that it had deposited certain amount passing of the decree it must be adjusted with the decretal amount and further the assurance given by the Decree-holder Bank, as submitted, being pending matter ; can be decided by the bank at any point of time but prior to sale of the mortgaged property and that the Decree-holder hank can satisfy its decree by adjustment of the amount deposited and the remission of interest. If any and requiring the judE4ment-debtor to pay the balance amount. if any, remain due after such adjustments and in turn release the property in favour of the Judgment-debtor. 
6. With the aforesaid observation the writ petition is disposed of without any order as to 
cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Mamtazuddin Ahmed, J:-This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-husband is directed against the judgment and decree dated 15.5.1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur, in Family Appeal No. 2 of 1992 affirming the judgment and decree dated 26.11.1992 passed by the Assistant Judge, Haimchar, in Family Suit No. 3 of 1992. 

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of the disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff filed the suit for restitution of conjugal rights on 27.4.1992 being family suit No. 2 of 1992 against the opposite party, wife. 

3. The wife being plaintiff who is opposite party herein instituted the suit for maintenance and for realization of dower money on 27.6.1992 being Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 against the above petitioner.

4. The husband being plaintiff in Family Suit No. 2 of 1992 stated that the plaintiff married the defendant on 22.11.1991 by registered kabinnama and dower money was fixed at Tk. 50,000/-and settled that husband will provide maintenance of Tk. 500/- per month. But due to mistake of the Nikah Registrar Tk. 3,000/- was written as maintenance in the kabinnama. The plaintiff as per settlement of the parties gave gold ornaments to the defendant. After the marriage they lived together as happy couple. On 6.2.1902 the plaintiff was in his working place at his school and on that day after coming home, came to know that the defendant (wife) left his house with ornaments and cash of Tk. 7,000/- along with her two brothers. The plaintiff at the evening on the same day went to his father-in-law's house and wanted to bring back his wife. And though his wife interested to come back but her relatives obstructed her to come to the house of the plaintiff and thereafter he instituted the suit for restitution of the conjugal rights being Family Suit No. 2 of 1992. 

5. The wife being plaintiff filed Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 and after the filing of the suit by husband. She stated inter alia that the dower money was fixed at Tk. 50,000/- and the maintenance at the rate of Tk. 3,000/- per months was fixed. At the time of marriage the father of the plaintiff gave ornaments and cloth of Tk. 33,000/- and also gave gifts amounting to Tk. 86,000/-. The husband did not pay the prompt dower at any time before or after the marriage and in spite of giving those dowry the husband put pressure upon the plaintiff, wife to bring Tk. 50,000/- as dowry and when she failed to meet up the demand, the husband driven her from his house on 6.2.1992 by keeping her belongings. The husband through his brother filed criminal case being No. 13 of 1992, in the Court of Magistrate, Haimchar, which was dismissed on 24.5.1992. In this way the defendant husband tortured the plaintiff and her father and her father and brothers both mentally and physically. Hence, she filed the suit.

 6. Family Suit No. 2 and Family Suit No. 3 were heard analogously by the learned Assistant Judge of the Family Court, Haimchar. The learned Assistant Judge dismissed the Family Suit No. 2 of 1992 for restitution of conjugal rights but decreed the suit for maintenance and dower filed by the wife. 

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree husband preferred appeal before the District Judge, Chandpur, against the judgment and decree passed in those suits. On transfer the learned Subordinate Judge 1st Court, Chandpur who heard the appeals and disposed of the same by single judgment and decreed the suit granted restitution of conjugal rights arose out of Family Suit No. 2 of 1992 and affirmed the judgment and decree passed in Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 for dower money and maintenance. 

8. The husband being plaintiff of Family Suit No. 2 of 1992 and defendant of Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 preferred this revisional application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present rule.

9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the husband petitioner has taken me through the judgments of both the Courts and submits that the Appellate Court committed error of law in affirming the judgment of the Trial Court in respect of dower money and maintenance and since the appellate Court decreed the suit for restitution of conjugal rights, in that case, affirming the judgment of the trial court passed in favour of wife for dower and maintenance committed fundamental error of law which has occasioned failure of justice. He submits further that whenever the appellate court decreed the suit for restitution of conjugal rights in that case the proper course would have been to execute the decree of restitution of conjugal rights as the marriage subsists and the question of payment of dower money and maintenance does not arise and in that position the appellate court committed error of law in affirming the judgment aid decree of the trial court which has occasioned failure of justice. 

10. Mr. Alam, again submits that the defendant (wife) has not challenged the decree for restitution of conjugal rights before this court and in that view also she is not entitled to get the execution of the decree as has been passed by the Trial Court which has been affirmed by the Appellate Court and as such the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court are liable to be set aside as it has caused failure of justice. 

11. Mr. Md. Abdul Quadir Talukder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party wife refuting the sub-mission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that though the opposite party has not preferred the revisional application against the judgment of the Appellate Court but this Court under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is entitled to take notice of the facts and to decide the same and even can rectify the error of law in a matter which has come to its notice or suomotu where the impugned order has been passed by a court subordinate to the High Court Division in which no appeal lies thereto. He submits further that the Appellate Court committed error of law in decreeing the suit for restitution of conjugal rights though the trial Court specifically found that the husband inflicted pains upon the wife and she also narrated the sad story of infliction of pains appearing before the Court and the learned Judge having seen the manner and demean our of the lady and evidences came to the findings that the husband really inflicted pains upon the plaintiff and for those reasons refused the prayer for restitution of conjugal rights but on those points the Appellate Court did not at all advert to the evidence though the lady stated personally appearing before the Trial Court and.in this view of the matter the learned Advocate urges for setting aside the decree of restitution of conjugal rights as is empowered under the provisions of the Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate court by giving such decree has allowed to spoil the youthful life of the lady which cannot be brought back as the same is concerned with life and in this way she lost about 10 years of her youthful. On the other hand, the petitioner got married and he is enjoying the life without taking this lady into his domain in spite of the decree passed by the appellate court and submits further urging the court to take notice of such painful fact and set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court in respect of the restitution of conjugal rights. He submits further that the trial court in refusing the decree for restitution of the conjugal rights and in decreeing the suit for maintenance committed no error of law and he urges for upholding the judgment of the Trial Court and set aside the judgment of the appellate court in respect of the decree for restitution of conjugal rights. 

12. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner has made submissions from different angle in respect of facts as well as law on the subject. 

13. During the submission upon a query from the court Mr. Alam has not been able to produce any paper to show that his client, the petitioner has taken any steps to bring the lady to his domain in spite of the decree passed by the appellate court in 1995 which apparently finds support of the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party, the wife. 

14. To this aspect of the case, I have examined the judgment of the appellate court and it has been found that the appellate court has not properly adverted to the evidences of the plaintiff (wife) of Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 wherein it appears that the lady plaintiff gave a vivid picture of the torture inflicted by the husband upon the plaintiff and caused injury and inflicted pains not only upon the lady but upon her father and brothers and the appellate court appears to have overlooked such evidence and given decree for restitution of conjugal rights which is not backed by evidences and thus committed error of law. 

15. Upon scrupulous scrutiny of the evidences it is found that the appellate court failed to exercise the jurisdiction as has been vested by the provision of law as the cause being related to life but not with the property and in view of the judgment of the appellate court the lady has lost 6 years of her youthful life without any fault of her own. The court whenever deals with such a case have to use the humane attitude towards problem and have to take into consideration that the problem relates to life but not with property. I have also examined the judgment of the Trial Court and it has been found that the trial court properly adverted to the evidences and legally refused the restitution of conjugal rights and apart from the evidence of torture, facts remain that the lady has lost more than 9 years of her youthful life, in view of the judgment of the appellate court but her such age can not be brought back by any kind of compensation. During this period it has been found further that the petitioner did not give her maintenance and take any steps to bring back the lady in his domain.

16. On perusal of the kabinnama, it appears that Tk. 3000/- was fixed for maintenance per month but the petitioner disputed the amount stating that it was not decided or written within his knowledge. It appears from the pleadings in the plaint that the petitioner stated that Tk. 5,00/- was fixed as maintenance instead of Tk. 3,000/- and stated further that the petitioner did not agree to give Tk. 3000/-as maintenance allowance but it was agreed upon at Tk. 500/- per month. In this score, I have also found the evidences on record. Though it was written Tk. 3,000/- per month, but circumstances led us to believe that a primary school teacher cannot afford Tk. 3,000/- per month as maintenance for his wife. I believe it was fixed at Tk. 500/- instead of Tk. 3000/- and in this view of the matter, petitioner before this court is liable to pay Tk. 500/- as maintenance allowance per month from July, 1992 to till today i.e. 30.7.2001. 

17. It is also on record that the Trial Court decreed the prompt dower and the appellate court also affirmed the same and in this aspect both the courts, it is found, committed no error of law. The wife will be able to bring separate suit for deferred dower if so advised. 

18. It is fact that the opposite party lady has not preferred the revisional application against the decree for restitution of conjugal rights but it has come to the notice of this court that in spite of the decree passed by the appellate court the petitioner: husband did not make any endeavor to bring back the lady to his domain which shows, the conduct of the petitioner that he is an unbecoming a per-son and disrespectful towards the man-date of the court and in view of the provisions under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, this court is also of the opinion that whenever any error commit-ted by subordinate to High Court Division in which no appeal lies thereto can rectify the error of law and even suomotu and such view finds support in the case of Ashwini Kumar Karmakar and others-Vs-Sudhir Kumar Chowdhury, reported in 38 DLR-39.

19. On scrutiny of the judgment of the Appellate Court it has been found that the Appellate Court has committed error of law in giving the decree of restitution of conjugal rights and whenever it has been brought to the notice of the court. I am of the view that this court can rectify the error of law and in that view of the matter this court on suomotu set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court as to the restitution of conjugal rights as the same having not been passed with proper consideration of evidences and the same in not backed by law. 

20. In view of my discussions and reasons stated above the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

21. In the result, the Rule is dis-charged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the appellate court in respect of restitution of conjugal rights are set aside. The plaintiff of Family Suit No: 2 of 1992 is directed to pay maintenance at the rate of Tk. 500/- from July, 1992 to 30.7.01 and also directed to deposit the same in the Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 of the Family Court, Haimchar, Chandpur and the petitioner is allowed to pay the same by 36 (Thirty Six) installments and Tk. 15,000/- may be deducted from the total amount of maintenance as the same appears to have paid to the lady. The petitioner is also directed to deposit the prompt dower of Tk. 19,000/- within five months from the date of receipt of this judgment and order, if not deposited in the meantime. 

22. The plaintiff of the Family Suit No. 3 of 1992 is entitled to draw the money from the court concerned. 

Send down the records at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Bijan Kumar Das, J.: This Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil procedure was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 20.5.1999 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Second court, Naogaon in title Appeal No. 192 of 1995 reversing those dated 5.8.1995 passed by the Assistant 
Judge, 3"1 Court, Naogaon in other class suit No. 171 of 1993 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted other Class suit No. 171 of 1993 in the 3rd Court of the Assistant Judge, Naogaon Sadar impleading the petitioner as defendant No.6 and opposite party Nos. 2-6 as other defendants praying for a decree for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of .01 decimal of land, as described in the schedule to the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to Afez alia Rafezudding and that C.S. Khatian No 92 was correctly prepared in his name along with his other co-sharers and the suit plot was recorded in the name of Rafezuddin alone and that Rafezuddin sold the suit land to the plaintiff and his brother by a kabala dated 6.7.1948 and plaintiffs brother Amiruddin filed an objection against the record under section 19(1) of 
state Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was allowed and S. A. Khatian was prepared in the name of plaintiff's brother and subsequently by amicable partition with' his brother the plaintiff got the suit land including other & lands, in all .06 acres, and the plaintiff was in possession 
of the same but R.S. Khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of Alekjan, the predecessor of the defendant and the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record of R.S. Khatian on 22.10.1992 when he went to the tahashil office to pay rents and due to such wrong record 
plaintiffs instituted other Class Suit No. 164 of 1992 and during pendency of the said suit the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff by violating the order of status quo from .01 acres of land on 2.12.1992. The plaintiff obtained a decree in other class Suit No. 164 of 1992 in respect of  .05 acres but no decree was passed in respect of 01 acres wherefrom the plaintiff was is possessed during pendency of the suit. the plaintiff accordingly filed the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession in respect of the aforesaid .01 acres land. 

3. The defendant No. 6 contested the suit by tiling a written statement contending, inter  alia, that the suit property along with other properties belonged to sontu Mondal, Shofog Mondal alias Afez Mondal and C.s. Khatian was accordingly prepared in their name and subsequently sontu Mondal died leaving behind 3 daughters in Alekjan, Khairren and Afjan and two brothers in Afez Mondal and shofez Mondal and that the said Khairun and Arian transferred their share to Alakjan who was in physical possession of the suit land since purchase. It is the further defence case that Afez and Shofez Mondal transferred their share to Alekjan by a registered Heba-bil-ewaz dated 27.31969 and that while in possession for over 20 years alekjan exchanged the land with defendant No. 6 by a registered deed of ewaz dated 1.12.1986 and the defendant erected several huts and has been possession the suit land. The contesting defendant also alleged that the plaintiff obtained an exparte decree beyond his knowledge for which he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1993 which was dismissed and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1993 was then filed which was pending. The contesting defendant further alleged that he got the suit land by a sale deed dated 6.7.1988 and that the plaintiff has no title or possession in the suit land and the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs. 
4. The trial court recorded evidence of 4 P. w s. and 3 D. w s. The plaintiff also produced  documentary evidence in support of his case though the defendant did not produce any ocumentary evidence. the trial court framed necessary issues and on consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the suit was not correctly valued and properly stampted and the suit was bad for defect of parties. The trial court then considered the issue with regard to plaintiffs title and possession and on consideration of the evidence came to the conclusion that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land. 

Accordingly by judgment and decree dated 5.8.1995 the learned senior Assistant Judge dismissed the plaintiff’s suit. 

5. The plaintiff then preferred Title Appeal No. 192 of 1995 before the learned District Judge, Naogaon, The Learned Subordinate Judge 2nd Court, Naogaon found that the trial court was not correct in holding that the suit was not legally valued and properly stamped and also the suit was not bad for defect of parties. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence came to the findings that the suit was not barred by res judicata as held by the trial court and further concluded that the plaintiff has proved his title and possession in the suit land. 

Accordingly by judgment and decree dated 20.5.1999 the learned subordinate Judge allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and decreed the plaintiff's suit. 

6. Being aggrieved thereby the defendant No. 6 being the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule. 

7. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has taken me through the judgments of the courts below and submits that the judgment of the lower appellate court is not a proper judgment of reversal. Mr. Goswami submits that the trial court has considered that the document of title of the plaintiff is an un-registered kabala dated 6.4.1948 and clearly found that the said which kabala could not be legally proved in evidence. Mr. Goswami further submits that the trial court has considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that the plaintiff could not prove his possession and subsequent dispossession in the suit land Mr. Goswami submits that the exparte decree passed in other class Suit No. 164 of 1992 with respect to .05acres of land would not be of any help to the plaintiff inasmuch as the suit being one for declaration of title and recovery of possession, onus lies heavily on the plaintiff to prove his title and possession and subsequent dispossession in order to obtain a decree for declaration of title and recovery of possession Accordingly to Mr. Goswami the plaintiff has miserably filed to prove his title and possession in 01. acres of land and subsequent dispossession there from. 

8. Mr. Abdus Samad Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, supports the decision of the lower appellate court and submits that the lower appellate court being the final court fact considered the evidence on record and held that the trial court was not correct in holding that the suit was bad for defect of parties or that the suit was not correctly valued and stampted. Mr. Samad further submits that the learned subordinate Judge being the final Court of the fact has considered the evidence and concluded that the plaintiff has proved his title on the basis of the un-registered kabala dated 6.7.1948 and has possession and subsequent dispossession and accordingly rightly reversed the decision of the trial court. Mr. Samad submits that the un-registered kabala dated 6.7.1948 has been accepted by the trial court in other class suit no. 164 of 1992 and the suit land being. 01 acres is a part and parcel of the land of the said kabala and that plaintiff acquired lawful title in the suit land on the basis of the un-registered kabala dated 6.7.1948 and the learned subordinate judge has rightly held that the plaintiff has title and possession in the suit. 

9. The plaintiff claims title on the basis of un-registered kabala dated 6.7.1948 The trial court has considered the un-registered kabala and found that the kabala was executed by putting LTI but LTI was not identified by anybody. It could not therefore be said that the un-registered kabala dated 6.7.1948 was executed by Rafezuddin by putting his LTI. These material aspect was not noticed was considered by the learned subordinate judge, the trial court has considered the evidence of p.w.2. Moyezuddin who came to prove the un- registered kabala and has refused to accept the evidence of P.W.2 on cogent ground. The trial court has also noticed that none of the attesting witnesses or the scribe of the kabala were examined in order to prove the kabala. Further the kabala being un-registered no title passed by the said kabala in favor of the plaintiff These aspect was not noticed and considered by the lower appellate court who reversed the decision of the trial court without reversing the material findings of the trial court with regard to acquisition of title by the plaintiff The trial court has not accepted the evidence of Pw. nos. 3 and 4 who came to prove plaintiff's alleged possession and subsequent dispossession. While discarding the evidence of p.w.3 and 4 the trial court has assigned sufficient reason. It appears that the lower appellate court decided the appeal on the weaken of the defense case without noticing the established principle of law that the plaintiff is required to prove its own casein order to get a decreeing a suit for declaration of title and of possession the plaintiff is required to prove his title and his possession and subsequent dispossession and also institution of the suit within 12 years from the date of alleged dispossession under article 142 of the limitation act. These legal aspect was not noticed and considered by the learned subordinate judge. The learned subordinate judge has however correctly held that the trial court was not correct in holding that the suit was not correctly valued and legally stamped with regard to defect of party the lower appellate court has referred to a decision in the case of Sher Mohammad and other w vs. Saroda Bala Sen and others reported in 45 DLR 527. In the said decision a single Bench of this court held only those persons who are in physical possession of the suit property should be made defendants and others are neither necessary nor proper parties in a suit for ejectment. The learned judge decided a matter under order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of civil procedure which arose out suit for ejectment of a tenant on the ground of default. The proposition of law laid down in the said decision of possession and the learned subordinate judge has not a legally applied the said decision in the instant case. The trail court has considered the question of possession and has considered the evidence of P.WS.1,2,3, and 4 and held that the plaintiff could not prove his possession and subsequent dispossession from the suit land. It is not disputed that other class suit No. 164 of 1992 was filed by the plaintiff in respect of 06 acres of land. It is the claim of the plaintiff that during pendency of the said suit the defendants dispossessed him from .01 acre of land. The trail court has noticed that the plaintiff filed a violation case being Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1993 which was dismissed by the trial court. It does not appear that the plaintiff took any step in other class suit No. 164 of 1992 to pray for recovery of possession in .01 acre of land by amending the plaint all these aspects were notice and considered by the trail court but the learned subordinate judge being the final court of fact has totally ignored to considered those material facts. I am therefore of the view that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal and needs interference by this Court. 

10. In the result this rule is made absolute without any order as to costs the impugned judgment and decree dated 20-05-1999 passed by the Subordinate Judge 2fid Court. Naogaon are hereby set aside and those dated 05.08.1995 passed by the Assistant Judge 3rd court Naogaon Sadar in other class suit No. 171 of 1993 restored. 

11. The order directing the parties to maintain status quo as passed at the time of issuance of the Rule is vacated.

End.

Mr. S. A. N. Mominur Rahman, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge-in-charge, Baliadangi, Thakurgaon in Title Suit No. 5 of 1992 decreeding the suit. 

2. The Opposite Party No. 1 hereof as plaintiff filed the suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of possession of the suit properties contending that he purchased the suit property on 7.4.92 by registered sale deed and there-after on 20th April. 1992, he got possession of the suit property. as agreed upon and then on 27.4.92 the defendant petitioner dispossessed the plaintiff who was possessing the suit properties through his employee Jaherucldin from the home-stead partition and then on 28th April, 1992 the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff from remainder of the property and hence he filed the suit on 16.8.92 for recovery of possession of the suit property. 

3. The defendant Nos. 2 and 7 con-tested the suit by filing joint written statement denying the materials allegations made in the plaint and contending that the suit property belonged to Dhaneswar, the grant father of the defendant No. 1 and father of defendant No. 7, and that defendant No. 1 married defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 6 is father of defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 7 is the daughter of Dhaneswar and that defendant No. 8 Dhaneswar Sinha did neither adopt Upendra Nath Sinha as dattak son nor transferred his properties in favour of Jitendra Nath Sinha son of Upendra Nath Sinha by way of gift but took care of defendant No. 1 and sent him to school and that the defendant No. 7 used to look after her aged father and inherited the property left by Dhaneswar and that said Dhaneswar bearer blind 3/4 years before his death. The defendant No. 8 appeared and filed written statement in the suit supporting the case of the plaintiff and thereafter on his death at Dhantala Upendra Nath Sinha substituted himself in place of defendant No. 8 Dhaneswar being defendant No. 8(ka) and filed written supporting the case of the plaintiff. The plaintiff adduced two witnesses including himself as P.W. 1 and employee Jaheruddin as P.W. 2. The defendant Nos. 1, 2, 6 and 7 adduced 5 witnesses and the defendant No. 8(ka) he himself deposed in the suit as D.W. 6. The learned Assistant Judge considering the evidence on record and the submissions made by the learned Advocates of the respective parties decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff has proved his possession in the suit land and also his dispossession from the suit properties on 27th and 28th April, 1992. The learned Assistant Judge also observed that the defendant did not challenge the gift made by Dhaneswar in favour of Jitendra Nath Sinha son of Upendra Nath Sinha by a registered deed dated 4.3.91 and that the defendant failed to prove that Dhaneswar was blind. 

4. Mr. S. S. Sarkar, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner for Mr. S. S. Haider, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner submitted that the learned Court below acted illegally in not considering the evidence on record of defendant and that the learned court below did not consider the deposition of the D.Ws. properly who supported the case of possession of Durgesh Chandra Sinha on the suit properties. The learned Advocate further submitted that in a suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of possession the plaintiff must prove his possession and dispossession clearly and specifically but in the instant case there is no witness to corroborate orate the story of dispossession of P.W. 2 Jaheruddin on 27.4.92 and the delivery of possession of the suit property to the plaintiff. The learned Advocate also sub-mitted that it has not been proved that Upendra Nath Sinha was the dattak son of Dhaneswar and that Dhaneswar gifted away the suit properties to Jitendra and therefore, on the death of Dhaneswar his daughter defendant No. 7 got the life-hold interest in the suit property and accordingly the defendant are in possession of the suit properties and the plaintiff was never in possession of the suit property. 

5. Mr. A. H. M. Mushfiqur Rahman. the learned Advocate on behalf of Mr. Md. Nazibar Rahman, the learned Advocate. appearing for the Opposite Party No. 1 submits that the finding of possession is a finding of fact and this court in its revisional jurisdiction should not interfere with such finding of fact as to possession inasmuch as there is no misreading or non-consideration of any evidence on -' record. The learned Advocate submits that that Dhaneswar took dattak the defendant No. 8(ka) and said Upendra Nath Sinha substituted himself claiming himself as dattak son of Dhaneswar in the spit itself, against which the defendant did not move the superior court and thereby they have accepted Upendra Nath Sinha as dattak son of Dhaneswar. The learned Advocate submitted that the defendant lid not challenge the gift dated 4.3.91 made by Dhaneswar in favour of Jitendra Nath Sinha and the same being valid in the eye of law, the subsequent sale of the suit properties in favour of plaintiff by registered deed dated 7.4.92 (Ext. 1) is also valid and stands good and the witnesses have proved the delivery of possession of the suit properties in favour of the plaintiff on 20th April, 1992, and that the plaintiff was possessing the suit properties through his employee Jaheruddin P.W. 2. The plaintiff has also proved through evidence that Jaheruddin was dispossessed from the homestead on 27th April, 1992 and thereafter the plaintiff was dispossessed from the remainder of the suit property on 28.4.92. The learned Assistant Judge on due consideration of the materials on record believed the case of the plaintiff and decreed the suit, holding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit properties. The learned Assistant Judge on due consideration of evidence on record also found that the plaintiff has been dispossessed from the suit properties on 27th and 28th of April, 1992, Dhaneswar find a written statement in the suit and on his death Upendra Nath Sinha as his substituted heir, also sub-mitted another written statement supporting the case of the plaintiffs said Upendra as D.W. 6 supported the plaintiff. The learned Advocate submits that in a suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act the title of suit property is not the main factor inasmuch as a person can maintain a suit under the said provisions of law to protect Lis possessory right. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Debendra Dahan Ds. Vs. Mohd. Afazuddin alias Afazuddin and others reported in 17 DLR Dhaka 387 wherein it has been held that even if the defendant has a better title then the plaintiff, he cannot resist and the plaintiffs suit of recovery of possession, if the plaintiff proved the allegation made by him. In the aforesaid case following paragraph from a Full Bench Case (Tamizuddin Vs. Ashraf All reported in DLR Cal. 647) has been quoted. The right to hold possession as against as illegal dispossession is one which in a possessory suit under Section 9 of the Specific Act is with any person who can prove an illegal dispossession. The law protects him against the illegal dispossession quite independently of any title on which he may claim to hold it. He has a right to remain there as against the dispossession even though such person may have a superior title. In a possessory suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act the question of title to the land in suit cannot be raised. 

6. I have perused the application, the impugned judgment and the materials on record. The learned Advocate for the petitioner took me through the depositions of all the witnesses adduced in the suit and also referred to the exhibits. I have perused the decision in the case reported in 17 DLR (Dhaka) 187 and I am in respectful agreement with the decision. It appears that the plaintiff claims the suit properties through Ext. 1 dated 17.4.92 and that the defendant has not challenged the aforesaid sale before any competent authority. It further appears that Dhaneswar Sinha, the admitted owner of the suit property transferred the suit properties in favour of the vendor of the plaintiff namely Jitendra Nath Sinha, by a registered Gift Deed dated 4.3.91 and the said gift has also not been challenged by the defendants in any court of law. It also appears that the aforesaid Dhaneswar was made party in the suit as defendant No. 8 who in due course appears in the suit and filed a written statement supporting the case of the plaintiff. Thereafter on his death Upendra Nath Sinha, claiming him-self as dattak son of Dhaneswar substituted himself in the suit as defendant No.8(ka) in place of Dhaneswar as heir and filed written statement supporting the case of the plaintiff and thereafter at the time of hearing he deposed in the suit as D.W. 6 supporting plaintiffs purchase and possession in the suit properties. The plaintiffs witnesses proved the sale deed Ext. 1 and also the delivery of possession of the suit properties on 20.4.91. It further appears that the learned Assistant Judge on due consideration of the materials on records of the case and discussions there-on found possession of the plaintiff into suit land on the strength of his purchase and that the plaintiff was on possessing the suit properties through P.W. 2 and has been dispossessed from the homestead portion in the suit land on 27.4.92 and from the remainder of the suit land on 28.4.92. It is the admitted position that the defendants No. 1-2 are in possession of the suit land at the present. There is nothing on record to show that the defendants entered into the suit land lawfully inasmuch as it is not the case that the defendant No. 7 got possession of the suit properties from her father amicably. Finding as to the possession is a finding of fact and finding of fact is not to be interfered with in revisional jurisdiction of this court unless there is any misreading or non-consideration of any materials on record, which is absent in this case. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and the provisions of Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act and relying on the decision recorded in 17 DLR Dhaka, 187. I do not find any reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree. 

7. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost of Taka. 2,000/ -. The impugned judgment and decree are affirmed. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule and extended thereby after till disposed of the Rule or is vacated... 

8. The petitioners is directed to deliver' possession of the suit properties in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 within 30 days of receipt of the case record by the learned Assistant. Judge, in default, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 will be at liberty to get possession of the suit proper-ties through the Court. 

9. Send down the lower courts records of the courts below immediately. 

End.

Mr. Abdus Salam Mamun, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite party No. 
1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 18.10.1993 (decree signed on 23.10.1993) passed by the Subordinate Judge, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 51 of 1999 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.2.1990 (decree signed on 1.3.1990) passed by the Assistant Judge, Manda in Other Class Suit No. 105 of 1980 renumbered as other Class Suit No. 569 of 1984 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order of orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts leading to issuance of this rules in short, are that the suit land was the jote land 
in the interest of Sree Ram Sarker under C.S.  Khatian No. 110. Sree Ram Sarker was succeeded by his two sons namely, Naddan Mistry and Narayan Mistry and the S. A. Khatian was recorded and published in their names. Upon a mutual partition among the brothers, Narayan Mistry got the right, title and possession of the suit land who has transferred the same to the proforma defendant No. 2 on 30.3.1979 under the registered deeds No. 5468 and 7243 respectively. The said proforma Defendant No. 2 has, after purchase, mutated her name and paid rent under separate Jama and on 21.5.1979 transferred the same to the plaintiff by executing a registered sale deed. But the defendant No. 1 threatened the plaintiff of dispossession from the suit land on 28.12.1979 who has no right, title and possession in the suit land and as such, the plaintiff has been obliged to institute the instant suit. 

3. The Defendant No. 1, by submitting a written statement, stated on the other hand that 
after death of Ram Chandra Sarker his sons Nandan Mistry and Narayan Mistry inherited 
the property to their equal shares and they were enjoying its possession. While Nandan Mistry was in right, title and possession of his share, transferred 161/2 satak of land out of 33 sataks in disputed plot No. 709 by a registered Danpatra No. 29.5.1979 and an area of .17 sataks of .34 
sataks in disputed plot No. 711 and another area of .10 sataks out of 1.21 sataks in the disputed plot No. 772, totaling 431/2 sataks and another 10 sataks in another plot to his daughter Sreemati Jotish Sarker, Jotish Rani Sarker, in her turn, transferred those .431/2 sataks of land to the defendant No. 1 the defendant No. 1 has also purchased an area of 071/2 sataks of land from Narayan Mistry on 8.6.1979 in plot Nos. 779, 709 and 711. The disputed property has not been partitioned by metes and bounds and the Bantannama that has been stated by the plaintiff, in his plaint is false, forged and manufactured one. The suit is also not maintainable for non-mentioning of Choudorddy (boundary) of the suit land. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge, Manda has framed the following issues in the suit. 
(1) whether the suit was maintainable in its present form: 
(2) whether there was any cause of action; 
(3) whether the plaintiff has any right, title and possession in the suit land; 
(4) whether the plaintiff was entitled to the reliefs, she prayed for. 

5. Upon taking evidence and assessment and appreciation of the same, the learned 
Assistant Judge was pleased to decree the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27.2.1990 and thereby restraining the defendant by way of permanent injunction. 

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Manda the defendant No. 1 has preferred the Title Appeal No. 51 of 1990 before the learned District Judge, Naogaon which was ultimately heard and disposed of by 
the learned Subordinate Judge (now the Joint—District Judge) First Court, Naogaon by his judgment and decree dated 18.10.1993 thereby allowing the appeal setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court. 

7. As against the said judgment and decree dated 18.10.1993 passed by the learned 
Appellate Court, the plaintiff respondent has preferred this Revisional Application under section 115 (1) of the code of the civil procedure and obtained the instant Rule. 

8. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned trial court on consideration and assessment of evidence on record found the plaintiff in possession of the suit land also found that her possession has been threatened by the defendant No. 1 and as such, passed the decree restraining the defendant No. 1 by way of permanent injunction. But the learned Appellate court without assessment and discussion of oral and documentary evidence on record has set aside the said judgment and decree holding that since the suit land was not partitioned, a suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. According to the learned Advocate, this finding of the learned Appellate Court is erroneous and liable to be set aside. 

9. Mr. Md. Mozaffar Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party No. 1, submits on the other hand that the plaintiff failed to prove any partition or demarcated possession in the suit land and evidence in this respect is contradictory so far it relates to the evidence of the P. W. 1 and 2 while the P. W. 1 claimed his possession through his wife, the P. W. 2 has stated otherwise and thus the factum of possession in this suit has not been proved and as the possession is not proved, the learned Appellate Court has not committed any error of law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, for, no decree for permanent injunction can be passed when possession of the plaintiff has not been specifically proved. 

10. Perused the application, heard the learned Advocates and examined the judgments of the Courts below together with the evidence and materials on record. It appears that the learned trial court has relied upon the evidence of P. W. 1 as well as D. W. 1 and 2 in respect of possession holding that the D. W. I and 2 have also admitted possession of the plaintiff. The learned trial Judge has also relied upon the mutation khatian and the separate Jama to consider the evidence of the P. W. 1 that the land in question had an amicable family partition and also construed that the separation of khatian amounts to partition and thus, passed the decree. The learned Appellate Court, on the other hand, held that in the plaint of the suit the plaintiff did not state any particulars of the alleged family partition and that from the evidence on record, it has not been proved that the defendant No. 1 is not possessing any land in the disputed plots and that the plaintiff also failed to prove her title. 

11. Both the learned Advocates are of their concurrent view that in a suit for permanent injunction, possession of the concerned party is the cardinal point to be decided in passing of a decree which is also the legal position. 

12. It appears that while the learned trial court held that the plaintiff-is in possession of the suit land, the learned Appellate Court held that the defendant No. I also cannot be said to be out of possession in the disputed plots. It further appears that the entire khatian i.e. the property of Ram Chandra Sarker and his two sons are not in dispute and it has also not been decided whether the parties are overlapping each-other. But apparently, the learned Appellate Court has not taken into consideration the mutation khatian and the separate jama which prima facie shows separate possession of the plaintiff in respect of the disputed land. The learned Appellate Court attempted to decide the title of the parties, which is not the fact in issue in the instant suit. 

13. The learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party pointed out the fact of not having the boundary of the disputed land in the plaint and submits that the learned Appellate Court has rightly found that the decree for permanent injunction cannot be passed where the boundary of disputed land has not specifically been stated in the plaint. Mr. S. N. Goswami, on the other hand, submits with reference to the exhibit 5 series and exhibit 6, which are rent receipts and mutation khatian in the name of the plaintiff—petitioner that these 2 exhibits have categorically identified the scheduled land of the plaintiff in respect of which she prayed for a decree for permanent injunction and as such the learned Appellate Court has taken an erroneous view in this respect. On perusal of exhibit-6 i.e. the mutation khatian and the exhibit-5 series i.e. the rent receipts in the name of the plaintiff–Petitioner, it appears that the disputed land has specifically and sufficiently identified, which is the basic purpose of mentioning the boundary in the plaint. 

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18.10.1993 (decree signed on 23.10.1993) passed by the Subordinate Judge, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 51 of 1990 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.2.1990 (decree signed on 1.3.1990) passed by the Assistant Judge, Manda, Naogaon in O. C. Suit No. (105 of 1980)/(569 of 1984)  is hereby set aside. The judgment and decree passed by the Learned Assistant Judge, Manda, Naogaon in O.C. Suit No. (105 of 1980)/(569 of 1984)  is hereby affirmed. 

The order of status–quo granted on 18.4.1994 at the time issuance of the Rule stands vacated. 

Send down the L. C. Record with a copy of this judgment to the concerned court at once. 

End.
